items.title: Kod
items.text:
Kod is a toy language that compiles to AArch64 (Apple Silicon) machine code for macOS. The self-hosted compiler (sh_kodc) compiles Kod programs, including itself.

func main() -> int64 {
    print("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

$ uv run kod build hello.kod
$ ./build/apps/hello/hello
Hello, world!

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Compiled to native ARM64 machine code (via as + clang)
  • Static types: int64, str, bool, arrays [T], structs, enums, optionals T?, generic types T[U, V] and functions f[T]
  • Union types: int64 | str, taken apart with n: int64 patterns
  • Pattern matching via match, plus if X is .Variant(bindings) sugar
  • F-string interpolation (f"hello {name}"), auto-to_str for non-string interpolands
  • Interfaces with vtable dispatch; primitives implement them via implicit boxing
  • Error handling via T or Error, try / must / throw
  • test "description" { ... } syntax with assert <expr> (source captured)
  • Modules and imports (import "kod/ast", import "./helper")
  • Self-hosted ARM64 codegen written in Kod itself

items.title: Status
items.text: The self-hosted compiler (sh_kodc) is the only implementation. A checked-in snapshot of it builds the current sources (see Self-hosting).

items.title: Writing an API client
items.text:
examples/github_repo.kod reads a repository's details and its open issues from the GitHub API. It is about a hundred lines and uses every piece of the standard library that a client needs; this page walks through it.

kod run examples/github_repo.kod anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python

anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python
  (no description)
  language: Python
  stars: 4030, forks: 901
  license: Apache-2.0
open issues:
  #2050 fix(streaming): keep compaction metadata when a delta omits encrypted_content
  #2049 fix(decoders): close the response when JSONL decoding fails
  #2048 fix(tools): don't coerce a non-object tool input in the session runner

Set GITHUB_TOKEN to send a bearer token (private repositories need one), and GITHUB_API to talk to something other than https://api.github.com. The tests use that to run the example against a local stand-in server (tests/support/http_fixture.py), so they need no network.

items.title: The pieces
items.text:
Arguments and environment. main(argv: [str]) receives the command line, with the program's name first. env.get("GITHUB_TOKEN") returns a str?, and x? or default handles a missing variable (Built-ins).

The client. What every request to the service needs goes on a Client once: its headers, its deadline. The example wraps it in a small GitHub type, so main reads as github.repo(name) and github.open_issues(name, limit: 3). One Client serves both requests, which keeps the connection from the first and uses it for the second (HTTP client).

let client = Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15))
client.headers.add("Accept", "application/vnd.github+json")
client.headers.add("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)

let response = try client.get(url)

A single request can override any of that with Options, for instance client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration(seconds: 2))). Client.get follows redirects, enforces the size limits and the deadline, and picks TCP or TLS from the URL.

Query strings. Build them with Query, which encodes names and values, rather than by joining strings:

let query = Query()
query.add("state", "open")
query.add("per_page", "3")
let url = with_query("/repos/" + name + "/issues", query)

Reading JSON. json.parse returns Value or Error. The accessors never fail, so a missing or null field is a fallback, not a crash:

func text_of(anon v: json.Value, key: str, fallback: str) -> str {
    return v.get(key).as_str()? or fallback
}

license.get("spdx_id") on a null license is Null, and as_str of that is none, which ? or "none" turns into the text none.

Errors. A non-2xx response is not a Kod error; fetch hands it back so you can read what the API said. The example turns it into its own ApiError and throws it, so that callers see one failure path for "the request failed" and "the API refused":

type ApiError = struct {
    status: int64
    reason: str
    detail: str

    func to_str(self) -> str { ... }
}

Network failures arrive as an IoError with a kind (ConnectionRefused, TimedOut, HostNotFound, Tls, Protocol, ...); see Streams. main here turns every failure into error: ... on standard error and an exit status of 1, and a bad command line into 2.

items.title: Sending JSON
items.text:
Writing to an API is the same, with a body. ObjectBuilder keeps the keys and values in step, and post sets the length and the content type:

import "json"
import "net/http" { post }

let body = json.ObjectBuilder()
body.put_str("title", "It crashes")
body.put_str("body", "Steps to reproduce: ...")
body.put("labels", json.array_of([json.str_value("bug")]))

let payload = kod_str_to_bytes(body.build().emit())
let response = try post(
    "https://api.example.com/issues",
    payload,
    content_type: "application/json",
)

items.title: What to know before relying on it
items.text:
• get, post and fetch open a connection for each request and close it. A program that makes many requests to one host should create a Client and call its get, post and fetch instead, which keep connections for reuse (Connection reuse).
  • timeout applies to the connect, the TLS handshake and each read or write. Set deadline to bound a request as a whole (Deadlines).
  • TLS goes through the system's SecureTransport, which speaks TLS 1.2 at most. A server that insists on TLS 1.3 fails with a Tls error.
  • Numbers with a fraction or an exponent come back as Decimal text: as_int() is none for them, as_number_text() gives the digits, and .parse_float() on those turns them into a float64.

items.title: Arrays
items.text: Arrays in Kod are resizable, homogeneous sequences. The type is [T] where T is the element type.

items.title: Literals
items.text:
let nums: [int64] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
let words: [str] = ["hello", "world"]
let empty: [int64] = []

A literal with no type to go to takes its first element's type, and every other element must have that type: let xs = [1, "a"] is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), and so is [Sq(s: 1), Circle(r: 1)] even when both implement Shape. Annotate the array to mix structs behind an interface: let shapes: [Shape] = [Sq(s: 1), Circle(r: 1)], which the error suggests when the module has an interface both implement.

items.title: Indexing
items.text:
let first: int64 = nums[0]
let last: int64 = nums[-1]    // negative index counts from end
let third: int64 = nums[2]

Negative indices wrap around: arr[-1] is equivalent to arr[len(arr) - 1]. An index must be an int64: nums["a"], nums[true] and an int64? index such as nums[m.get(k)] are errors.

Arrays nest: an element of a [[int64]] is an [int64], so grid[i][j] and for row in grid { for x in row { ... } } work, and an element of a [bool] is a bool.

A literal takes its element type from where it goes, at any depth: a let, an assignment, an argument, a field, an enum payload, a return value (including a match arm's), the rest of an array + chain (see Concatenation), or an element or Map value it's stored as. In let g: [[Shape]] = [[Sq(s: 3)]], shapes += [Sq(s: 4)], [Sq(s: 1)] + shapes or return [none, 3] from a -> [int64?] function, each struct is boxed as the interface and each value wrapped as the optional. In a [Direction], [.North, .South] builds Direction variants even when another enum declares variants of those names, and in a [Maybe[int64]], [.Just(value: 1), .Nothing] builds Maybe[int64] ones.

Arrays, str and bytes can be indexed, and so can a struct that declares an op_index method (Map does). Element assignment needs an array or a struct with op_index_set, slicing needs an array, str or bytes, and for … in needs an array. Anything else is a compile error.

An assigned element must have the array's element type, with the same conversions as a let: names[0] = 5 on a [str] is an error, while xs[0] = 42 on an [int64?] and pets[0] = Cat() on a [Pet] wrap and box the value. On a struct, the key of m[k] and the key and value of m[k] = v must have the types of op_index's and op_index_set's parameters (see Indexing a struct), so m[5] on a Map[str, int64] is an error.

A store evaluates its parts left to right: in rows()[i()] = v() and m[k()] = v() the receiver comes first, then the index or key, then the value, and f().x = v() calls f before v. A compound rows()[i()] += v() evaluates the receiver and the index once, reads the element and then evaluates v(), so rows and i are each called once. Indexing a struct calls its op_index, so it counts as a call too: xs[a[k]] += b[k] calls a's op_index once, before b's.

items.title: Length
items.text: let n: int64 = len(nums)

items.title: Slicing
items.text:
let sub: [int64] = nums[1..4]   // elements 1, 2, 3
let prefix: [int64] = nums[..3]  // first three
let suffix: [int64] = nums[3..]  // from index 3 onward
let copy: [int64] = nums[..]     // shallow copy

Both endpoints clamp to [0, len]: a negative bound becomes 0 and a bound past the end becomes len, so [1, 2, 3][1..10] is [2, 3]. An end before the start yields an empty slice. Unlike indexing, slice bounds never wrap. Both bounds must be int64.

items.title: Concatenation
items.text:
Use += to append elements or extend with another array:

mut a: [int64] = [1, 2]
a += [3, 4]          // a is now [1, 2, 3, 4]

Or + to produce a new array; neither operand is modified:

let b: [int64] = [5]
let c: [int64] = a + b   // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; a and b are unchanged

Every literal and match in a chain of + is built as the type the whole chain goes to, or, without one, as its first operand that isn't a literal or match. So [Sq(s: 1)] + [Sq(s: 2)] + shapes boxes both squares as Shape, and let ms: [Maybe[str]] = [.Just(value: "a")] + [.Nothing] builds Maybe[str] variants. The other operands must all have that one type: squares + shapes (a [Sq] and a [Shape]) and nums + names are errors, and so is names + [1], whose literal's element isn't a str.

+= grows the array's buffer geometrically, so appending in a loop is amortized O(1) per element. + always copies both operands, so xs = xs + [x] costs O(len(xs)); prefer xs += [x] in loops. xs += [x] with one element builds no array for the literal: x goes straight onto the end of xs.

+= appends to the array itself, not to a copy, so everything that holds the same array sees the new elements: after let a = xs and xs += [3], a ends in 3 too. That holds for an array kept in a field or in another array (rows[0] += [4]) as well, and for an array passed to a function that appends to its parameter. A for x in xs loop also reaches the elements appended to xs while it runs.

The one exception is a mut binding that starts from an existing array, a variable, a field or an element: it gets a copy of its own, so appending to it leaves the original alone.

mut ys = xs            // a copy of xs
ys += [4]              // xs is unchanged

A mut binding that starts from a call, a literal or an expression such as xs + [] already holds an array nobody else has, so nothing is copied. To keep the old contents in any other case, copy the array first with xs + [] or xs[..]. All of these copies are shallow: the inner arrays of a [[T]] are still shared.

items.title: Iterating
items.text:
Index-based:

let i: int64 = 0
for i < len(nums) {
    print_int(nums[i])
    i = i + 1
}

Foreach:

for n in nums {
    print_int(n)
}

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
Arrays are represented as a header struct on the heap:

{ void* ptr, int64 len, int64 cap }

The ptr field points to a block of elements, each 8 bytes wide. len is the number of live elements; cap is the allocated capacity.

Appending (+=) goes through _kod_array_concat in the runtime, which writes into the existing buffer and reallocates it with doubled capacity only when cap runs out. + goes through _kod_array_concat_new, which allocates a fresh header and buffer.

items.title: Helpers
items.text:
The arrays module has what's the same for an array of any type:

import "arrays"

arrays.contains(["a", "b"], "b")     // true
arrays.equal([1, 2], [1, 2])         // true

Elements compare with ==, so strs by content, and a type that == doesn't take is an error (see Generic functions).

items.title: Sorting
items.text:
The sort module's functions return a new array and leave the argument as it is. They take O(n log n) comparisons and are stable: elements that compare equal keep their order.

import "sort"

sort.sorted([3, 1, 2])       // [1, 2, 3]
sort.sorted(["b", "a"])      // ["a", "b"]

sorted orders by <, so it takes numbers, strs (by byte), and structs that declare op_lt. sorted_by takes the order as a function that says whether its first argument goes before its second:

sort.sorted_by(people, less: func(a: Person, b: Person) -> bool {
    return a.age < b.age
})

items.title: Built-ins
items.text:
These names live in stdlib/builtins.kod and are available in every Kod program without an explicit import.

A call without a module name, f(args), goes to the first of these that exists:

  1. a struct named f that the module sees (Pt(x: 1) constructs);
  2. the innermost binding of f in force, when it holds a function value;
  3. a function the module declares or lists in an import;
  4. the builtin of that name.

A binding that holds anything else doesn't hide a function, so let len = len(xs) and a later len(ys) both call the builtin. It does hide any outer binding of its name: after let g = double, a call g(1) in a block that binds let g = 5 goes to the module's or the builtin g. With neither, it is an error: `g` is a local of type `int64`, not a function.

A function value declared in a block hides an outer one only inside that block; after the block, f(args) calls the outer one again. With no binding of f in force and no function of that name, the call is an error: `f` is called before its `let` or `f` is declared in a block that has ended; declare it outside the block to call it here.

The same holds for len, str, hash and panic: a module can declare its own func hash(anon p: Point) -> int64, and its hash(...) calls use it, while another module's dep.hash(x) names that one. An f-string always converts its values with the builtin str. Only the builtin panic counts as a call that never returns; a module's own or imported panic, or a local function value of that name, is an ordinary call. A local named panic that holds anything else doesn't hide the builtin, so panic(msg) after let panic = 5 never returns.

items.title: Output
items.text: Function Signature Description print (x) -> none Print x, followed by a newline. Takes whatever f"{x}" does (see Strings). print_int (int64) -> none Print an integer followed by a newline. Equivalent to print(n.to_str()). kod_puts (str) -> int64 Write a string and a newline to stdout. What print calls; embedded NULs are written as-is. putchar (int64) -> int64 C putchar: write a single byte to stdout. Shares libc's stdout buffer with print.

items.title: Length
items.text:
Function Signature Description len (str) -> int64 String length in bytes. len ([T]) -> int64 Number of elements in an array. len (SomeStruct) -> int64 Dispatches to the struct's func len(self) -> int64 method if one exists (e.g. Map.len); a len method of any other shape is an error.

As a value, len is its string form: let n: func(str) -> int64 = len.

items.title: Bytes
items.text:
Function Signature Description kod_str_to_bytes (str) -> bytes The same bytes, typed bytes; nothing is copied. kod_bytes_to_str (bytes) -> str The same bytes, typed str; nothing is copied. kod_bytes_from_array ([int64]) -> bytes One byte per element, from its low 8 bits. kod_bytes_le64 (bytes, int64) -> int64 The 8 bytes from at as one int64, the first byte lowest (little-endian). An at below 0, or fewer than 8 bytes left, panics with the index of the first missing byte.

kod_bytes_le64(b, at) is what reading the 8 bytes one at a time and shifting them together gives, in one load: a decoder reading many bits at a time uses it to fill its bit buffer.

items.title: String conversion
items.text:
There is no int_to_str builtin — primitives carry their own to_str methods:

let s: str = 42.to_str()      // "42"
let t: str = true.to_str()    // "true"
let u: str = "hi".to_str()    // identity

F-strings interpolate non-str values by calling to_str automatically:

print(f"n = {42}")            // n = 42

items.title: Hashing
items.text:
let h: int64 = "hello".hash()
let g: int64 = 99.hash()

int64.hash is the identity function; str.hash is djb2; bool.hash is 0/1. Used internally by Map[K, V].

The hash(x) builtin takes a hashable value: an int64, str, bytes or bool, a value of an enum whose variants have no payloads, which hashes by variant, or a value of a union whose members are all hashable, such as int64 | str. Hashing anything else, such as a struct, an array, an optional or an enum with payload variants, is an error (cannot hash a value of type `[int64]`), as is hashing a union with a member that can't be hashed, which the error names (cannot hash a value of type `[int64] | int64`; its member `[int64]` can't be hashed). It gives what the methods above give, a bytes value hashes like the str with the same bytes, an enum value hashes to its variant's position, counting from 1, and a union value hashes the member it holds, mixed with which member that is, so the int64 0 and the bool false don't collide.

items.title: Map[K, V]
items.text:
A built-in generic. Open-addressing hash map (PEP 468 dense + sparse).

let m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()
m.set("a", 1)
m.set("b", 2)
match m.get("a") {
    Some(v) -> print(v.to_str())
    none -> print("miss")
}
print(len(m).to_str())   // 2
Method Description set(k, v) Add k with value v, or replace the value k has. m[k] = v is the same. get(k) -> V? k's value, or none when k isn't in the map. m[k] is the same. contains(k) -> bool Whether k is in the map. remove(k) -> V? Take k out of the map, giving the value it had, or none when it wasn't there. keys() -> [K] / values() -> [V] The keys, or the values, in the order the keys were first set, as a new array. len(m) How many keys the map holds.

The entries keep the order their keys were first set in: setting a key again changes its value but not its place, and a key that is removed and set again goes last. for k in m and for k, v in m go over them in that order (see for / in). set, get, contains and remove take constant time on average.

A lookup finds the entry whose key is == to the one it's given, so key equality depends on the key type: str and bytes keys match by content, int64 and bool keys by value, enum keys by variant, and union keys when they hold the same member and those are equal, so in a Map[int64 | str, V] the keys 1 and "1" are two keys.

The key type must be hashable, as for hash(x): int64, str, bytes, bool, an enum without payload variants, or a union of those. Any other key type, such as Map[[int64], int64], Map[int64?, str] or a struct, is an error at the type argument that names it, in whichever module it's written (`[int64]` can't be a `Map` key), reported once per key type. A key that comes from another generic type's parameter is reported at the argument of that type that is or holds the key: with type Index[V, K] = struct { m: Map[K, V] }, a parameter of type Index[int64, Pt] is an error at Pt (`Pt` can't be a `Map` key in `Index[int64, Pt]`). A Map[T, V] in a generic type's method names the instance whose T is the bad key (`Pt` can't be a `Map` key in `Box[Pt]`); any other bad key in a method, such as a Map[Pt, int64] written out in Box[Pt], ends with the instance it's compiled for, as other errors there do ((in `Box[Pt]`)). The same holds for the element type of a Set[T] from the sets module.

items.title: Indexing a struct
items.text:
m[k] calls the struct's op_index and m[k] = v its op_index_set, which is how Map supports both (m[k] is a V?, like m.get(k)). op_index must take one key besides self, and op_index_set a key and a value:

func op_index(self, anon key: K) -> V? { ... }
func op_index_set(self, anon key: K, anon value: V) -> none { ... }

The key and value must have those parameters' types, like a method's arguments. m[k] = v evaluates m, then k, then v before the call, and m[k] += v calls op_index and then op_index_set with the same m and k, each evaluated once.

items.title: Error handling
items.text: Name Description Error (interface) Marker for types that can be thrown. Requires to_str(self) -> str. ExitCode (interface) exit_code(self) -> int64, declared but not consulted yet: an Err that main returns exits with status 1 whatever it implements. panic Print panic: <msg>\n to stderr and exit(1). Used by must and by assert outside a test. kod_eprint (extern) Write to stderr without exiting.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Name Description fail(msg) Mark the current test "..." {} as failed; outside a test, no-op. assert <expr> Statement form. Inside a test, flag on false; outside, panic. Source text is captured at parse time. See Testing.

items.title: I/O
items.text:
The io module wraps the filesystem primitives. Both calls require import "io" — touching the filesystem is explicit at the import line.

import "io"

// Read the whole file. Pipes and FIFOs (e.g. "/dev/stdin") are read
// until EOF. Returns "" if the file can't be opened or read.
let contents: str = io.read_file("data.txt")

// Write a file, replacing it if it exists. Returns 0 on success,
// -1 on failure. The parent directory must already exist.
let rc: int64 = io.write_file("out.txt", "hello\n")

For subprocess support, see stdlib/process.kod:

import "process"

let r: process.ProcessResult = process.run(["echo", "hello"])
assert r.status == 0
assert r.stdout == "hello\n"

process.run(argv) captures stdout and stderr. process.spawn(argv) starts argv[0] (looked up on PATH) without waiting for it, with stdin, stdout and stderr on /dev/null, and returns its process id, or -1 when it could not be started. process.kill(pid) ends a child that spawn started, with SIGTERM, waits for it, and returns whether it was signalled; a child that is never killed stays a zombie until the parent exits. process.exec(argv) instead replaces the calling process with argv[0], looked up on PATH: the new program has the same terminal, stdin and process id. Stdout is flushed first. If stdin is a pipe, input the program has already read into its buffer (as io.read_stdin_line does, beyond the line it asked for) is not handed on; a file or a terminal loses nothing. exec returns, with -1, only if argv[0] could not be run.

import "process"

func main() -> int64 {
    process.exec(["echo", "hello"])
    return 127  // not reached unless `echo` could not be run
}

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
stdlib/env.kod reads and changes the process's environment. A program's arguments come from main(argv: [str]) (see Functions).

import "env"

func main() -> int64 {
    let token = env.get("API_TOKEN")
    print(token? or "no token")
    env.set("MODE", "test")
    env.unset("API_TOKEN")
    return 0
}
Function Meaning get(name) -> str? the value, or none if the variable isn't set; a variable set to the empty string is "", not none set(name, value) -> none or Error set or replace it; the change is seen by programs started afterwards with process.run and process.exec; an empty name, one containing = or a NUL byte, and a value with a NUL byte are InvalidInput errors unset(name) -> none remove it; unsetting a variable that isn't set does nothing

items.title: Extern (C runtime)
items.text:
Available for re-declaration in any module if needed:

Symbol Description _strlen C strlen. _rc_alloc Allocates an object with a reference count of 1; see Memory layout. _kod_str_concat, _kod_str_slice String operations the runtime exposes to codegen. _kod_sb_new, _kod_sb_append, _kod_sb_append_byte, _kod_sb_len, _kod_sb_clear, _kod_sb_to_str The growable buffer behind StrBuilder and the str methods join, repeat, replace, lower and upper; a handle is typed as a str so that it is counted, but isn't one. _kod_fd_open, _kod_fd_read, _kod_fd_write, _kod_fd_close, _kod_io_errno, _kod_errno_kind, _kod_errno_message Descriptor I/O and OS error numbers behind stdlib/posix.kod and stdlib/stream.kod; see Streams. _kod_array_concat, _kod_array_concat_new Array append in place (+=) and concatenation into a new array (+). _kod_test_fail, _kod_test_summary Test runner internals. read_file, write_file File I/O.

Direct use is rarely needed — the language-level operators cover most cases.

items.title: CLI reference
items.text: The CLI is kod (installed as a project script). Run it as uv run kod ... from the repository root: it refreshes the toolchain with make and hands off to the native tool build/apps/kod/kod. From any other directory it prints one line saying where to run it from and exits 1.

items.title: kod build <file>
items.text:
Compile a Kod source file to a native ARM64 binary.

uv run kod build hello.kod
./build/apps/hello/hello

Build pipeline:

  1. Refresh the toolchain with make stage1 kod (a no-op unless the compiler, the C runtime, or an always-linked stdlib module changed). This only happens when kod runs from the repo root; invoking build/apps/kod/kod directly skips it. If the rebuild fails, kod reports it and stops.
  2. Parse the entry and walk its transitive imports. A missing entry file (path:1:1: error: no such file) or a missing import (importer:line:col: error: no such module ...) is an error. Then read the comment lines at the top of each module for the C files, link arguments and required files it declares (Link inputs); a mistake in them, or a required file that isn't there, stops the build before anything is compiled.
  3. Compile each module that isn't prebuilt in build/stage0/ to a .o with sh_kodc _compile, the entry first, stopping at the first that fails, and then each C file the modules name, once. A module compiled before is taken from build/cache/ instead: its object there is named by a SHA-256 of sh_kodc, the module's path, and the path and text of each module it loads (what it imports, directly or not, and the STAGE0_KOD modules), which is all its object depends on. So an unchanged module isn't compiled again, whichever program it's in. Only modules named by a relative path, inside the project, are kept there. A failing module's errors follow those in the declarations of the modules it loads, such as an import that names no file, an unknown return type, a field declared twice or a parse error, since its own may be only their cascades.
  4. Generate and assemble the _main runtime shim that calls the user's main.
  5. Link everything against the prebuilt build/stage0/ objects with the LINK command of link.cfg (clang, see Self-hosting), followed by the arguments the modules give with kod:link. The driver reads link.cfg, and link.local.cfg if there is one, from the working directory: run it from the repository root, or it says link.cfg not found.

The native driver (build/apps/kod/kod, built from tools/kod.kod) runs steps 2–5.

A syntax error is reported once: the parser skips the rest of the statement, struct field, parameter or declaration it is in, and carries on with the next, so a later mistake is still found. A missing , between parameters, or a missing : before a field's type, is taken as written. Type errors inside a declaration (a function, a type, a constant) that has a syntax error aren't reported, since they may come from what the parser skipped; the other declarations are checked as usual.

On a terminal, errors are coloured: the location and message in bold, error: and the caret under the column in red. Set NO_COLOR to any non-empty value, or TERM=dumb, to turn colour off. When stderr is a file or a pipe there is none.

items.title: kod run <file>
items.text:
kod build + execute. Arguments after the file are passed to the program.

uv run kod run hello.kod

kod replaces itself with the program (execvp), so the program has your terminal. Its stdin, stdout and stderr are yours, its output appears as it is written, and its exit status, or the signal that killed it, is what your shell sees. (stdout is block-buffered when it is not a terminal; call io.flush_stdout() where the order of the two streams matters; a panic flushes it before its message.) If the program cannot be executed, kod says so and exits 127.

items.title: kod test <path>
items.text:
Run test "..." { ... } blocks. Path can be a file or a directory.

  • File: builds the file + all transitively-imported modules that contain tests, runs everything in one binary, prints a rolled-up summary.
  • Directory: walks for *_test.kod and builds them all into one program, with no temporary module, so two test files may share a file name. A file with a path component below the directory that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files) and a build directory directly below it are skipped; a *_test.kod that cannot be read (a link to nothing) stops the run. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.
uv run kod test stdlib/map_test.kod
uv run kod test stdlib            # everything under stdlib/
uv run kod test .                 # everything in the project

Both replace kod with the test binary, as kod run does with a program: its output appears as it is written and its exit status is kod's. The test reporter flushes stdout around every result line and before a failure's detail goes to stderr, so the ok/FAIL lines and the assertion failed detail stay in order on a pipe or in a CI log too; output a test prints itself is flushed with them.

See Testing for the syntax.

items.title: kod check <file>
items.text:
Run the full compile pipeline through codegen, report errors, but write no artifacts and skip the link step. Exits non-zero on any error. It also checks the link directives at the top of each module (see Link inputs), but compiles no C file and does not look for a kod:require file. An error already shown for one module isn't shown again for another.

uv run kod check src/foo.kod

items.title: Build outputs
items.text:
Path Description build/stage0/ The objects sh_kodc, kod and every app share: the C files and Kod modules link.cfg lists as RUNTIME_C and STAGE0_KOD (arena.o, rc.o, runtime.o, _<name>.o; see Self-hosting) and the compiler library the two tools link. build/stage1/ The self-hosted compiler sh_kodc and the objects it is linked from (kodc.{s,o}, runtime_main.{s,o}). build/apps/<stem>/ The final executable, <stem> (or <stem>_test for kod test). <stem> is the entry's file name without .kod; for kod test <dir> it is the directory with every byte outside letters, digits, _ and - replaced by _ (its last 200 bytes, when it is longer), then _tests. A file whose name without .kod is empty, . or .. has no program name and is refused. An entry named kod or lsp (other than tools/kod.kod and tools/lsp.kod, however they are spelled) is refused, because its executable would replace the tool. So is one whose directory the volume takes for the tool's, such as KOD on a case-insensitive volume. build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/ The program's objects, in a tree that mirrors the source tree: each module's .o, with its .s when it was compiled rather than taken from the cache (lib/json.kod is <stem>.obj/lib/json.kod.o), the object of each C file a module names (<stem>.obj/lib/json.c.o) and the _main shim (<entry>.main.{s,o}, or <first entry>.testmain.{s,o} for tests). So json and ./json, or a/util and b/util, are different objects.

| build/cache/ | Module objects by key (step 3), <sha256>.o. Rebuilding sh_kodc empties it, since every key names the compiler. |

make clean-apps (which also empties build/cache/), make clean-stage1, make clean give scoped cleanup.

items.title: Internal / debug commands
items.text: These exist for the build and for debugging. Their shape may change: sh_kodc has the internal subcommands _compile, _emit-runtime-main and _emit-test-runtime-main.

items.title: if / else
items.text:
if x > 0 {
    print("positive")
} else {
    print("non-positive")
}

The else branch is optional. Braces are always required.

The condition must be a bool. There's no truthiness, so if n on an int64 is an error (write if n != 0), and so is if x on an optional (write if x is not none, or if x is Some(v) to bind the value).

items.title: for (while-style)
items.text:
for with a condition loops until the condition is false:

mut i: int64 = 0
for i < 10 {
    print_int(i)
    i = i + 1
}

This is Kod's general looping construct. There is no while keyword. As with if, the condition must be a bool.

The condition can bind names as an if condition does, alone or joined by and. The loop ends when a pattern fails, and the names are new each time round:

for reader.next_line() is Some(line) and len(line) > 0 {
    print(line)
}

items.title: for / in (foreach)
items.text:
Iterate over an array with for … in:

let names: [str] = ["alice", "bob", "carol"]
for name in names {
    print(name)
}

The loop variable is declared implicitly — no let needed.

for i, x in xs also numbers the elements from 0:

for i, name in names {
    print(f"{i}: {name}")
}

for i in a..b counts from a up to but not including b, like the slice xs[a..b]. Both bounds must be int64 and are evaluated once, before the first iteration, so changing n in the body of for i in 0..n doesn't change how many times it runs. a..b works only here: it isn't a value of its own.

for i in 0..3 {
    print_int(i)    // 0, 1, 2
}

Either form can take _ for a name it doesn't use.

A str or bytes value is iterated byte by byte, each byte an int64 from 0 to 255, as s[i] gives it; for i, b in s numbers them. For text, iterate over s.code_points() instead.

mut spaces: int64 = 0
for b in "a b c" {
    if b == ' ' {
        spaces += 1
    }
}

A Map is iterated in the order its keys were first set: for k in m gives the keys and for k, v in m each key with its value. The loop goes over the entries the map had when it started, so the body may set and remove entries freely.

for name, age in ages {
    print(f"{name} is {age}")
}

A Set from the sets module is iterated the same way, for x in s, over its elements in the order they were first added.

Arrays, str, bytes, Map, Set and a..b can be iterated; any other kind of value is an error.

items.title: break and continue
items.text:
Works inside both loop forms:

let i: int64 = 0
for i < 100 {
    if i == 5 {
        break
    }
    i = i + 1
}

for x in items {
    if x == skip_value {
        continue
    }
    process(x)
}

items.title: match
items.text:
Pattern matching on enums, integers, and strings. See Pattern matching.

match direction {
    Direction.North -> print("north")
    Direction.South -> print("south")
    else -> print("other")
}

items.title: Blocks and bindings
items.text:
A statement ends at the end of its line or at a }, so two statements can share a line only after a block (if c { a() } b()). Anything else after a statement on its line is an error: let x = 5 print_int(x).

A let or let-else binding lasts from its statement to the end of the block it's in. The bindings of a match arm's pattern, or of if … is, last for that arm. A for … in variable lasts for the loop body, and parameters (self included) for the whole function. Parameter and field defaults follow the same rules.

Every block has its own scope. A binding may take the name of one still in force, whatever kind of binding either is: a let, mut or let-else, a name in a pattern, a for variable, a parameter or self. Inside its block, arm or loop body the new binding hides the old one, and reading or assigning the name there means the new one. When that block, arm or loop ends, the old binding is back with its own value, type and mutability:

func show(anon item: A, anon flag: bool) -> str {
    if flag {
        let item = B(x: 9)   // hides the parameter until the `}`
        return item.show()   // B's show
    }
    return item.show()       // A's show
}

mut total = 0
for x in xs {
    let total = x * 2        // this loop body's own `total`
    print(f"{total}")
}
total = total + 1            // the `mut total` again

A block may also bind a name again itself. The new binding then replaces the old one for the rest of that block. These count as binding the name again in the same block:

  • a function's top block reusing a parameter's name;
  • an arm reusing its pattern's name;
  • a loop body reusing its for variable's name.

A binding's value, the array of a for … in and the value that if … is tests all see the binding the name had before, even when the type differs: let x = x + 1, let x = f"#{x}", for x in x, if o is Some(o). A let-else's else block runs when the pattern doesn't match, so there the name still has the binding it had before the let-else:

for arg in args {
    let .Some(arg) = parse_num(arg) else {
        print(f"bad: {arg}")   // the str from `args`
        continue
    }
    total += arg               // the parsed int64
}

A name is a local only where a binding of it is in force. Elsewhere it means a function of the module, an imported one or a builtin of that name, as it does in a call (see Function values). Elsewhere means before its let, or after the block, arm or loop that bound it when no outer binding is in force. With none of those functions, reading or assigning the name is an error: `x` is read before its `let` or `x` is declared in a block that has ended. When another module declares a type of that name and this one doesn't see it, reading or calling the name gives the error for that type (unknown type `Mode`; lib/modes.kod declares `Mode`: write `modes.Mode` or list it in the import (`{ Mode }`)), as with no local at all. Assigning the name still gives the errors above. Declare a name before the block to use it after the block:

mut label = "other"
if n > 0 {
    label = "positive"
}
print(label)

A function literal doesn't see the locals of the function it's written in.

items.title: return
items.text:
Return a value from a function:

func abs(n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n < 0 {
        return 0 - n
    }
    return n
}

A bare return (no value) is valid in -> none functions.

A function that returns a value must not be able to run off the end of its body (see Return values). An if without an else, a for over a condition or an array, and a for true loop with a break can all finish, so a return has to follow them; a match whose arms all return, and a for true loop that only leaves through return, can't. Nor can a call that never returns: panic(...), or a -> none function or method without a return whose body can't finish by these same rules, such as one that ends in another such call or in a for true loop without a break. A method counts whatever it's called on, a local included, as long as the receiver's type is known at the call. A call through a function value and a method called through an interface value are taken to return, since what they call is chosen at run time; end such a path with a panic(...) or a return after the call (see Return values).

items.title: Base64
items.text:
stdlib/encoding/base64.kod implements RFC 4648 base64, in both the standard alphabet (A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) and the URL-safe one (- _ in place of + /).

import "encoding/base64"

let text = base64.encode_str("Aladdin:open sesame")
// QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==

let raw = must base64.decode("QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==")   // bytes
let back = base64.decode_str("QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==")    // str or Error
Function Meaning encode(data: bytes, url: bool = false, pad: bool = true) -> str the base64 text of data; url: true uses the URL-safe alphabet; pad: false leaves out the trailing = encode_str(s: str, url: bool = false, pad: bool = true) -> str the same for the bytes of a str decode(text: str, url: bool = false) -> bytes or Error the bytes text stands for decode_str(text: str, url: bool = false) -> str or Error the same, as a str (the bytes are not checked to be UTF-8)

Encoding is exact for any bytes, including NUL, and takes linear time.

Decoding is strict, so that two texts never stand for the same bytes by accident and a mangled input is noticed:

  • only the chosen alphabet is accepted: + and / are errors with url: true, and - and _ are errors without it;
  • no whitespace or line breaks are skipped (this is not MIME base64);
  • padding is optional, but if it is there it must be exact: Zg== and Zg are both f, while Zg=, Zg===, Z===, =Zg= and Zg==Zg== are errors;
  • a length that leaves a single character over (Zm9vY) is an error;
  • the unused bits at the end must be zero, so Zh== (whose last character carries bits that f would not set) is an error.

Errors are IoErrors of kind InvalidInput, with op base64 decode and a detail that names the byte offset of the problem where there is one.

items.title: Compression
items.text:
stdlib/compress/deflate.kod compresses into the three formats that compress/inflate reads, written in Kod like it.

import "compress/deflate"

let packed = deflate.gzip(kod_str_to_bytes(text))
let quick = deflate.gzip(data, level: 1)
Function Meaning gzip(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a gzip file (RFC 1952) of one member, with no name and a zero time zlib(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a zlib stream (RFC 1950) raw(data: bytes, level: int64 = 6) -> bytes a raw deflate stream (RFC 1951)

level trades speed for size as zlib's does: 0 only frames the data (stored blocks), 1 to 3 take the first good match, and 4 to 9 look further back and put off a match when the next byte starts a longer one; 9 is the smallest and slowest. A level outside 0..9 is taken as the nearest one. Each block is written whichever way is smallest: stored, with the standard codes, or with Huffman codes made for its own data, so data that doesn't compress grows by only about 5 bytes every 16 KB.

items.title: Decompression
items.text:
stdlib/compress/inflate.kod decompresses gzip, zlib and raw deflate data. It is written in Kod, like compressing, so it links no C library.

import "compress/inflate"

let text = kod_bytes_to_str(must inflate.gunzip(data))
Function Meaning gunzip(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a gzip file (RFC 1952); several members one after the other give their output joined, like gunzip does inflate_zlib(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a zlib stream (RFC 1950) inflate_raw(data: bytes, max_output: int64 = 16777216) -> bytes or Error a raw deflate stream (RFC 1951)

max_output is the most bytes the result may have. Decompression stops as soon as it would be exceeded, so a few kilobytes of input cannot make the program allocate gigabytes; the buffer grows only as output is produced. Errors are IoErrors of kind InvalidInput, with op the function's name and a detail that says what was wrong: output too large, truncated, or the wording zlib uses for corrupt data (incorrect header check, invalid block type, incorrect data check for a checksum that does not match, incorrect length check, invalid distance too far back). Bytes after the last gzip member are an error, and so is a stream that ends before its final block.

items.title: Percent-encoding
items.text: For URLs and query strings, see HTTP client.

items.title: Enums
items.text: Enums in Kod are tagged unions — each value carries a discriminant identifying which variant it is, plus an optional payload with named fields.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
type Direction = enum {
    North
    South
    East
    West
}

type Message = enum {
    // unit variant (no payload)
    Quit
    // payload variants
    Text(content: str)
    Move(x: int64, y: int64)
}

Comments are allowed inside the body. Variants without parentheses are unit variants; variants with parentheses carry named fields.

A payload field can name the enum itself, e.g. Branch(kids: [Tree]) inside type Tree = enum { ... }.

items.title: Construction
items.text:
let d: Direction = Direction.North
let m: Message = Message.Text(content: "hello")
let q: Message = Message.Quit

The annotation is optional: a constructor has the enum's type, so let m = Message.Text(content: "hello") (or mod.Enum.Variant(...) for an imported enum) can be matched without an else arm.

Payload values go in declaration order, labelled or not: Message.Move(x: 1, y: 2) and Message.Move(1, 2) are the same value. A missing or extra payload value, a label that isn't the field in that position, and a variant the enum doesn't declare (Message.Txt) are errors. Each payload value must have its field's type, with the same implicit conversions as a function argument: Message.Text(content: 5) is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`).

items.title: Implicit variant syntax
items.text:
Inside a match arm, the enum name can be omitted when the type is unambiguous:

match d {
    .North -> print("north")
    .South -> print("south")
    else -> {}
}

The variant must belong to the subject's enum: .Up in a match on a Direction that has no Up is an error, even when another enum declares Up, and so is naming that other enum, Arrow.Up. The same goes for an if d is ... pattern.

Unit variants can also use the implicit .Variant form in expressions:

let d: Direction = .North

A payload variant can use it too. Wherever the enum type is known, the variant belongs to that enum: an annotated let (let m: Message = .Text(content: "hi")), an assignment to a variable, field, element or key, an argument, a struct field, an array element, an array literal in a + chain with an array of the enum (ms += [.Quit], [.Quit] + ms or [.Quit] + [.Text(content: "a")] + load()), a return value (the T of a T or Error function too), the other side of == or != (m == .Quit), in a comparison chain too (.Quit == m == n), or an arm of a match whose value goes to one of these (d == match n { 0 -> .North else .South }). Elsewhere, as in an unannotated let, a match subject, an unannotated array literal or a method call on the variant, it belongs to the one enum that declares a variant of that name among those the module sees: its own, those of the modules it imports and the builtin ones. When several of them declare it, that is an error:

type Figure = enum {
    Square(side: int64)
    Circle(r: int64)
}

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(r: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

let s = .Circle(r: 2)
// error: `.Circle` is ambiguous: `Figure` and `Shape` both declare it;
// write `Shape.Circle` or give the value a type

let s: Shape = .Circle(r: 2) and Shape.Circle(r: 2) both work. The error writes an imported enum through its import alias, as in geo.Shape, so when the module's own Shape and an imported geo.Shape both declare Circle, the error names Shape and geo.Shape. It suggests an enum whose variant takes the payload written (a unit variant for a bare .Circle), preferring the module's own enum when several do. Enums of modules a module doesn't import don't count, so a generic method or a default written in an imported module means the same variant whichever program uses it. Only when none of the enums the module sees declares the variant does an enum of another loaded module count. When several of those do, the module can't write any of them, so the error only suggests giving the value a type, as by passing it straight to a parameter of its enum.

In a T or Error function, a returned .Ok(...) or .Err(...) is the result's own variant, unless T declares a variant of that name whose payload fits what is written and the result's doesn't. With type Status = enum { Ok Failed(code: int64) }, return .Ok in a -> Status or Error function returns Status.Ok, while return .Ok(.Failed(code: 1)) returns the result's Ok. When both variants take the one argument written, its type decides: with Ok(n: int64) in Status, return .Ok(5) returns Status.Ok(n: 5), as 5 can't be a Status. An arm of a returned match works the same way, and so does a return type that names the T or Error through an alias.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Declare methods inside the enum body, after the variants. The first parameter is self, the enum value:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(r: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)

    func area(self) -> int64 {
        return match self {
            .Circle(r) -> 3 * r * r
            .Rect(w, h) -> w * h
        }
    }

    func scaled(self, by: int64) -> Shape {
        return match self {
            .Circle(r) -> .Circle(r: r * by)
            .Rect(w, h) -> .Rect(w: w * by, h: h * by)
        }
    }
}

let s: Shape = .Rect(w: 2, h: 3)
print(s.scaled(by: 2).area())    // 24

They take arguments, labels and defaults like struct methods, work through s?.area() on a Shape?, and can be called on any Shape value, including one that came from a function in another module without your module importing the one that declares Shape. A method whose name starts with _ is private to the enum's own methods, as on a struct.

An enum that declares func to_str(self) -> str is printed by it in f-strings and print, instead of by its variant's name.

A generic enum declares methods the same way, and they use its type parameters:

type Either[L, R] = enum {
    Left(value: L)
    Right(value: R)

    func swapped(self) -> Either[R, L] {
        return match self {
            .Left(value) -> .Right(:value)
            .Right(value) -> .Left(:value)
        }
    }
}

As with a generic struct, a method is compiled for an instance when something calls it, only its signature is checked otherwise, and an error in its body names the instance, as in (in `Either[int64, str]`).

An enum gives operators a meaning with the same operator methods as a struct: op_add, op_sub, op_mul, op_div, op_mod, op_eq, op_lt and the reflected op_radd and the rest. An enum that declares op_eq is compared by it, payloads and all, so == and != work on any two of its values, including a .Variant on the right:

type Amount = enum {
    Cents(n: int64)
    Free

    func op_eq(self, other: Amount) -> bool {
        return self.cents() == other.cents()
    }

    func op_lt(self, other: Amount) -> bool {
        return self.cents() < other.cents()
    }

    func cents(self) -> int64 {
        return match self {
            .Cents(n) -> n
            .Free -> 0
        }
    }
}

let a: Amount = .Cents(n: 0)
print(a == .Free)                // true
print(a < .Cents(n: 5))          // true

An enum without op_eq keeps comparing variants, as described under Equality.

An enum that declares an interface's methods is a value of that interface, as a struct is (see Interfaces), and an interface value holding one downcasts to it with if v is Dir(d) or a Dir(d) arm:

interface Named {
    func name(self) -> str
}

type Dir = enum {
    Up
    Down

    func name(self) -> str {
        return match self {
            .Up -> "up"
            .Down -> "down"
        }
    }
}

let n: Named = Dir.Down
print(n.name())                  // down

A generic enum's instance is one too, and downcasts through a type alias such as type IntPick = Pick[int64], as a generic struct's does.

items.title: Generic enums
items.text:
Type parameters go in square brackets after the name, as for structs, and each instantiation is monomorphised:

type Either[L, R] = enum {
    Left(value: L)
    Right(value: R)
}

let e: Either[int64, str] = .Left(value: 1)

A variant of a generic enum needs its type arguments from where it goes: an annotated let, as above, or any other place listed above where the enum type is known, such as an argument, an array element or the other side of ==. Without one, let e = Either.Left(value: 1) (or .Left(value: 1), Result.Ok(5)) is an error, cannot infer the type of `e`; add a type annotation. Type arguments on the enum name, Either[int64, str].Left(value: 1), are an error, since type arguments must be followed by (. A pattern names the enum without them, and its bindings take the matched value's payload types: on an Either[int64, str], Either.Left(n) binds an int64.

items.title: Pattern matching
items.text:
match m {
    Message.Quit -> print("quit")
    Message.Text(content) -> print(content)
    Message.Move(x, y) -> {
        print_int(x)
        print_int(y)
    }
    else -> {}
}
  • Bindings in payload patterns (content, x, y) capture the field values
  • else is the catch-all arm; matches whatever the other arms didn't
  • Arm bodies can be a single expression (after ->) or a block ({ ... })

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
[ offset 0  ] discriminant : int64  (8 bytes)
[ offset 8  ] payload      : max(variant payload sizes) bytes

Variants are assigned discriminants in declaration order starting from 1. Discriminant 0 is reserved as the none sentinel.

items.title: Example: Message
items.text:
Message.Quit  → discriminant 1, no payload
Message.Text  → discriminant 2, content at payload offset 0  (8 bytes)
Message.Move  → discriminant 3, x at offset 0, y at offset 8 (16 bytes)

Total size: 8 (discriminant) + 16 (max payload) = 24 bytes.

items.title: Equality
items.text:
Two enum values are equal if and only if they are the same variant. Payload contents are not compared. An enum that declares op_eq is compared by that method instead (see Methods).

Direction.North == Direction.North  // true
Direction.North == Direction.South  // false

In the compiler this is a single integer comparison on the discriminant.

Since payloads aren't compared, an enum with payload variants only compares with a variant that has none: with m: Message, m == .Quit and m != Message.Quit are fine, but m == .Text(content: "hi") is an error that suggests m is .Text(content) instead, and so is comparing two Message values (a == b); test them with is or match. Comparing values of two different enums is an error, and so is a .Variant that the other side's enum doesn't declare.

items.title: match as an expression
items.text:
A match can produce a value when every arm has a value: an expression, or a block ending in one:

let label: str = match d {
    .North -> "north"
    .South -> "south"
    .East  -> "east"
    .West  -> "west"
}

Payload bindings are in scope in the arm's expression:

let dist: int64 = match m {
    .Move(x, y) -> x + y
    else 0
}

items.title: Floating point
items.text:
float64 is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating-point number, the type of every JSON number that is not a whole number.

let price: float64 = 19.99
let total = price * 3.0 + 0.5
print(total.to_str())            // 60.47

items.title: Literals
items.text:
A float literal has digits on both sides of a point, an exponent, or both:

1.5
0.25
2e9
6.02e23
1.5e-3
1 000 000.5          // grouped like an integer

1. and .5 are not literals: a point needs a digit after it, so that 1.to_str() still calls a method on the integer 1. Nothing else turns an integer into a float; 2 is an int64 and 2.0 is a float64.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
Operator Operands Result + - * / two float64 float64 -x a float64 float64 < <= > >= == != two float64 bool

Nothing converts implicitly: 1.5 + 1 and n * 0.5 with n: int64 are errors, and so is % on a float. Arithmetic follows IEEE 754 exactly, so 1.0 / 0.0 is infinity, 0.0 / 0.0 is not a number, and a not-a-number value is unequal to everything, itself included (x != x is how to test for one, or x.is_nan()). There is no trap on overflow or division by zero.

A float64 is an ordinary value: it can be a variable, parameter, field, array element ([float64]), optional (float64?) or a type argument (Box[float64]). It cannot be a Map key or a Set member, because its == is not an equivalence, and it has no literal pattern in a match.

items.title: Conversions and methods
items.text:
Method Result n.to_float64() on an int64 the nearest float64 x.to_int64() x truncated toward zero; a not-a-number is 0 and an out-of-range value saturates to the int64 limits x.to_str() the shortest text that reads back as x (below) s.parse_float() on a str a float64?: none unless all of s is a decimal number, with an optional sign, a point and an exponent; inf, nan and hex are not accepted x.abs() x.floor() x.ceil() x.round() x.sqrt() the float64 they name; round rounds halves away from zero x.is_nan() x.is_inf() bool

to_str gives the fewest digits that parse back to exactly x (rounded half to even from its exact value, when more than one such text has that many digits), and always shows it is a float: 2.0, not 2. Magnitudes from 1e-6 up to 1e21 are written without an exponent (0.000001, 123456789.5); outside that range as 1e+21 and 1.5e-7. The special values are inf, -inf and nan. An f-string uses to_str; print takes a str, so write print(x.to_str()).

parse_float gives the float64 nearest the decimal value, however many digits it has; a value exactly halfway between two floats goes to the one whose last bit is 0. A value beyond the largest float is infinity, and one below half the smallest is zero, with the sign kept. Both directions are Kod, in stdlib/primitives/float_text.kod, with exact arithmetic on integers wider than 64 bits where a float can't be trusted.

print((0.1 + 0.2).to_str())     // 0.30000000000000004
print((1.0).to_str())           // 1.0
print(("2.5e3".parse_float()?).to_str())   // 2500.0

items.title: JSON
items.text:
A JSON number that is not a whole int64 keeps its text in a Decimal, so reading one as a float is parse_float on that text, and writing one is to_str:

let text = item.get("price").as_number_text()?
let price = text.parse_float()?
let out = json.Value.Decimal(text: (price * 1.2).to_str())

to_str gives text that is a valid JSON number for every finite value. Infinity and not-a-number have no JSON form: emit writes a Decimal whose text is not a number as null, so inf and nan come out as null.

items.title: Representation
items.text: A float64 is the 8 bytes of its bit pattern, held in an ordinary register or slot; the compiler moves it to a floating-point register only for the operation. That is why it needs no new calling convention and an array of them is an array of 8-byte words.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
func add(a: int64, b: int64) -> int64 {
    return a + b
}

Parameters are name: Type. The return type follows ->. Functions that return nothing use -> none.

Every argument is passed in a register, so a function can take at most 8 parameters. self takes one of them, so a method or interface method can take at most 7 besides self. The same limit holds for externs, function literals and function types such as func(int64) -> int64, in a type alias too; going past it is an error where the function, literal or type is written (`f` takes 9 parameters, but a function can take at most 8), not again at each call through it. When that is in another module, the error is reported at each call through it instead. To pass more, group them in a struct.

items.title: Calling
items.text:
let result: int64 = add(1, 2)

The arguments are worked out left to right, each once, before the body runs. A small function or method whose whole body is return of an expression made of its parameters, literals, operators and field reads, with int64, bool or float64 parameters (a method's self may be a struct) and result, like add above or a method func area(self) -> int64 { return self.w * self.h }, is compiled in place at each call instead of being called. So is a short body of statements (let of a number or bool, assignments, if, for with a condition, break, continue, return and calls, but no match, for x in, try, is or function literal) whose parameters, none of them mut, are numbers, bools or structs, and whose result is a number, a bool or nothing; a struct argument must then be a local name, as self must. It behaves the same, except that a backtrace from inside it, such as a division by zero, names the caller.

items.title: Call labels
items.text:
Calls use labeled arguments by default; the parameter name is the label:

func greet(name: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
}

greet(name: "Alice")

Labeled arguments go in parameter order: with func move(x: int64, y: int64), move(y: 2, x: 1) is an error (parameter 0 of `move` expected label `x`, got `y`). A label may jump over parameters that have defaults, which are then left out of the call.

anon removes the label requirement for that parameter:

func double(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    return n * 2
}

double(5)

Convention: when calling, label every parameter except 1–2 of a single shared type (e.g. slice(arr, from: 0, to: 3) is fine; passing a label for arr is just noise).

If a passed argument is a bare identifier with the same name as the parameter, the label can be shortened to a leading ::

let name: str = "Alice"
greet(:name)          // shorthand for greet(name: name)

items.title: Long calls and parameter lists
items.text:
A call may be split across lines wherever the arguments are separated, and so may a parameter list. Put each argument on its own line, with or without a trailing comma, and comments between them:

let conn = connect(
    "example.com",
    port: 8443,        // not the default
    timeout_ms: 200,
    tls: true,
)

func request(
    anon method: str,
    anon url: str,
    timeout_ms: int64 = 5000,
) -> none { ... }

This holds for every call: functions, methods, x?.method(...), struct and enum constructors (Point(x: 1, y: 2)), and the argument lists of enum variants in a type declaration. A line break after the callee and before the ( still ends the statement, so f and (1) on two lines are two expressions, not a call. A call that never closes is reported at the first token that cannot continue it, for instance expected `)`, got `let` on the line of the next statement.

items.title: Label / binding split
items.text:
A parameter can have two names — an external label used at call sites and an internal binding used inside the function body:

func greet(who person: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {person}!")
}

greet(who: "Alice")

Useful for prepositions that make call sites read naturally without forcing short variable names inside the function.

Each parameter binds a name of its own, self included, so two parameters can't share one: func f(anon a: int64, b a: str) is an error (parameter `a` is declared twice; give one of them another name). The same holds for methods, interface methods, externs and function literals.

items.title: Default values
items.text:
Trailing parameters may declare a default with = expr, and a call can leave them out:

func retry(anon n: int64, delay_ms: int64 = 100) -> int64 {
    return n * delay_ms
}

retry(3)                  // 300
retry(3, delay_ms: 500)   // 1500

The default is evaluated fresh at each call that omits it. It is evaluated in the module that declares the function and can't see the caller's local variables, so a name in it means the same thing at every call site. Methods and interface methods take defaults the same way. A default must have its parameter's type, like an argument. A function's or method's default has its type checked where it is declared, so func f(x: int64 = "a") is an error even if no call leaves x out. Anything else wrong in it, such as an unknown name or variant, or a wrong field in a constructor, is reported where a call leaves it out, and an interface method's default is checked only at each call that leaves it out.

A label can jump over parameters that have defaults, so that a later one can be set without writing out the ones in between:

func connect(anon host: str, port: int64 = 80, timeout_ms: int64 = 5000, tls: bool = false) -> none { ... }

connect("example.com")                          // all defaults
connect("example.com", timeout_ms: 200)         // port and tls by default
connect("example.com", port: 8443, tls: true)   // timeout_ms by default

The labels still go in parameter order, and a parameter that is jumped over must have a default; connect(port: 1) is an error because host has none (parameter 0 of `connect` is anon; remove label `port`). An anon parameter with a default can be jumped over the same way, by labeling a later argument. Unlabeled arguments fill the parameters strictly in order, so only a label can skip.

Each default is evaluated afresh at the call, in the order of the parameters, along with the arguments you did give: in f(a: x(), c: z()) for func f(a: int64, b: int64 = y(), c: int64 = 0), the calls run x, then the default y, then z. It works the same for methods, interface methods and functions of other modules.

items.title: Argument types
items.text:
Each argument must have its parameter's type: print(5) is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`), and so is passing a Gen[int64] where a Gen[str] is declared, or an int64? where an int64 is. The only implicit conversions are the ones an annotated let makes (see Bindings and mutability):

  • a T becomes a T?;
  • a struct, int64, str or bool becomes an interface value;
  • .Variant and Enum.Variant(...) are built for the parameter's enum;
  • an array literal or + chain is built for an array of enums, interfaces, optionals or arrays.

An array value is never converted element by element. With func take(anon xs: [Shape]), take([Sq(s: 1)]) is fine, but passing a [Sq] variable is an error. The same rules apply to extern functions, to calls through a function value, and to the arguments of a method, an interface method and x?.method(...).

items.title: Return values
items.text:
A returned value must have the function's return type, with the same conversions as an argument: func f() -> str { return 5 } is an error (expected `str`, got `int64`), and so is returning a [Sq] variable from a -> [Shape] function. A -> none function returns no value; it can end with a bare return, return none, or return of a call that itself returns none. Any function can return a call that never returns (see below), such as return self.fail("bad") or return log.die("bad").

In a -> T or Error function, a returned T becomes a successful result. A returned T or Error value must have the same T, so returning an int64 or Error from a -> str or Error function is an error.

A function with a return type other than none must end every path with a return, a throw, or a call that doesn't return, like panic(...). One that can reach the end of its body is an error at its name, or at the func of a function literal (`pick` can reach its end without returning a value), and that includes a -> T? function: write return none at the end. Only a -> none or Error function may run off its end, which returns Ok(none). The error isn't reported for a body that already has other errors, or in a file that doesn't parse, since those may hide the missing return. Whether a path can reach the end is decided from the statements alone:

  • return, throw, break and continue end a path, and so does a call of a function or method that never returns;
  • an if ends every path only if it has an else and both branches do;
  • a match does if each of its arms does;
  • a for true loop does unless it can break out of itself; any other for loop, including for … in, may finish.

Code after a statement that ends every path is never run and isn't considered, so a break placed after a return or panic(...) doesn't let a for true loop finish.

The builtin panic(...) never returns, and neither does a function or method that returns none, has no return, and can't reach the end of its body by these rules. A function of the module or one it imports named panic, or a local function value of that name in force at the call, hides the builtin (see Built-ins). A local named panic that holds anything else doesn't, so panic(msg) after let panic = 5 never returns. So a helper that ends in panic(...) never returns, and nor does one that ends in a call of another such helper (self.fail(msg), log.die(msg), or a function declared further down), or in a for true loop it can't break out of. A call that leads back to the function itself doesn't count: func spin() -> none { spin() } is taken to return.

This holds for a call of:

  • a function of the module or one it imports (die(msg)), or a function of an imported module (log.die(msg));
  • a method of a struct, whatever it's called on: self, a parameter, any local, a field or a call's result (self.fail(msg), self.log.fail(msg), r.fail(msg), self.reps[i].fail(msg), reporter().fail(msg)), as long as that expression's type is known at the call. A local has the type of its binding in force there, whether a let, let-else, match arm, if … is or for binds it, so r.fail(msg) never returns after let r = Reporter(), even where r is also a parameter of another type.

Two kinds of call are always taken to return, because what they call is chosen at run time:

  • a call through a function value (a local, parameter or field of a function type);
  • a method called through an interface value.

End such a path with a panic(...) or a return after the call.

A call in a value's place, as a returned value, a match arm's value or an x? or ... default, is decided where it is written by the same rules, so return r.fail(msg) never returns after let r = Reporter(), and nor does return die(msg) when die ends in that call. When what it calls ends in a call taken to return, the error names that call and its line: return die(msg) is an error when die ends in r.fail(msg) after let r: Failer = Reporter(), for an interface Failer (as `die` ends in `r.fail(msg)` (line 19), or (line 19 of lib/log.kod) when the call is in another module), and it says to put a panic(...) after it. The can reach its end error names that call too when the body ends in a call of such a function, and says so when the body itself ends in a call through a function value or a method called through an interface value. Such a call is taken to return wherever it is written: call it as a statement and end the path with panic(...).

items.title: main
items.text:
Every executable must define main. It can take no arguments or receive the command-line argument list:

// no args
func main() -> int64 {
    return 0
}

// with argv
func main(argv: [str]) -> int64 {
    print_int(len(argv))
    return 0
}

main can also return int64 or Error, directly or through an alias. A returned value is the exit status, and an error that reaches the end of main prints panic: <message> and exits with status 1.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Functions inside a struct type declaration are methods. The first parameter must be self:

type Counter = struct {
    value: int64

    func increment(self) -> none {
        self.value = self.value + 1
    }

    func get(self) -> int64 {
        return self.value
    }
}

Call with dot notation:

let c: Counter = Counter(value: 0)
c.increment()
print_int(c.get())

items.title: Function values
items.text:
Functions are values. Use func(T1, T2) -> R as a type to store, pass, or return them. A function value is an 8-byte reference, not a C function pointer (see Function values).

func double(x: int64) -> int64 { return x * 2 }
func triple(x: int64) -> int64 { return x * 3 }

func apply(anon f: func(int64) -> int64, anon x: int64) -> int64 {
    return f(x)
}

let g: func(int64) -> int64 = double
print_int(g(21))             // 42 — indirect call through g
print_int(apply(triple, 14)) // 42 — function passed as callback

A function literal, func(anon n: int64) -> int64 { return n + 1 }, is a value of its function type too.

A bare identifier in value position resolves to the function's address when no local of that name is in force there. A call f(args) goes to a struct named f first, so Pt(x: 1) constructs. Otherwise it does an indirect blr when the innermost binding of f in force holds a function value, and a direct bl of the module's, an imported or the builtin function named f when no binding of f is in force or it holds anything else. A function value declared in a block, such as an if or loop body, is called that way only from its let to the end of the block, and after the block f(args) calls an outer function value of that name again. Elsewhere f(args) calls the module's or an imported function, or the builtin, named f, and f as a value is that function; with none of those it is an error: `f` is declared in a block that has ended after the block, and `f` is called before its `let` (or read) before the declaration (see Blocks and bindings and Built-ins).

A function of an imported module is a value written through its module, let f = vec.dot. A name the module doesn't declare is an error with a did-you-mean hint (module `vec` has no function or constant `dott`).

An indirect call has the function type's return type wherever the function value comes from: a local, an array element (fs[i](x)), a struct field (h.fn(x)) or another call (get_fn()(x)). It must pass exactly as many arguments as the function type has parameters, since a function type carries no defaults.

items.title: Closures
items.text:
A function literal can read the locals and parameters in force where it's written, including self. It keeps their values, so it can outlive the function that made it:

func adder(anon n: int64) -> func(int64) -> int64 {
    return func(anon x: int64) -> int64 {
        return x + n
    }
}

let add5 = adder(5)
print_int(add5(1))           // 6

A literal captures the value a name has when the literal is evaluated. Each pass of a loop makes its own closure, with that pass's for variable and pattern bindings. Literals nest, and an inner one can capture what the outer one can see.

A variable declared mut is shared instead: the literal and the function it's in use the same variable, so what one assigns the other sees, even after the function has returned:

func make_counter() -> func() -> int64 {
    mut n = 0
    return func() -> int64 {
        n += 1
        return n
    }
}

let next = make_counter()
next()
print_int(next())            // 2

A mut declared in a loop's body is a new variable on each pass, so each pass's closure has one of its own. Any other name the literal captures keeps the value it had when the literal was evaluated, and can't be assigned in it: a function literal can't assign to `x`, which it captures. That holds for a let, a parameter, a for variable and a pattern binding. A mut parameter can't be captured: a function literal can't capture `p`, a `mut` parameter; copy it into a `mut` local to share it.

A captured mut lives in a counted cell from its declaration on, and each read and assignment of it goes through the cell, in the function too; a mut that no literal captures stays in the frame.

Other limits:

  • A literal can't see its own let, so it can't call itself through it. Use a named function to recurse: unknown function `fact`; a function literal can't see its own `let`, so use a named function to recurse.
  • A literal inside a generic function, or a method of a generic type, can't capture: a function literal in a generic function or type can't capture `x`. Passing a closure to a generic function works, as in sort.sorted_by(xs, less: ...).
  • A default value sees no locals, so a literal used as one captures nothing.
  • A closure kept in a struct that it captures is a cycle, and a cycle is never freed (see Reclaiming memory).

items.title: Generic functions
items.text:
Type parameters in brackets after the name make a function generic. They can be used in its parameters, its return type and its body:

func first[T](anon xs: [T]) -> T? {
    if len(xs) == 0 {
        return none
    }
    return xs[0]
}

func map_all[T, U](anon xs: [T], f: func(T) -> U) -> [U] {
    mut out: [U] = []
    for x in xs {
        out += [f(x)]
    }
    return out
}

let a = first([1, 2])                                      // a: int64?
let b = map_all([1, 2], f: func(anon n: int64) -> str {    // b: [str]
    return f"#{n}"
})

Like a generic struct, a generic function is monomorphised: it's compiled once for each list of type arguments a module calls it with.

items.title: Inference
items.text:
A call usually leaves the type arguments out, and the compiler works them out from the arguments:

  • Arguments are read in parameter order. Each one is matched against its parameter's declared type: T takes the argument's whole type, [T] an array's element type, Box[T] an instance's type argument, and func(T) -> U a function's parameter and return types. T? takes the inner type of an optional or else the argument's own type, so int64? and int64 both make T an int64.
  • The first argument to settle a type parameter decides it. Later arguments are then converted to the parameter's type as in any call, and one that can't be is an error at that argument. With func pick[T](a: T, b: T), pick(a: 1, b: "x") reports expected `int64`, got `str`, and arguments of two structs that share an interface need the type written out, as in pick[Shape](a: sq, b: circle).
  • An argument with no type of its own (none, [], .Red) settles nothing, but takes its type from the parameter once the others have settled it: with func add[T](xs: [T], x: T), add(xs: [], x: 1) makes T an int64.
  • A parameter left to its default settles nothing either.
  • Only arguments count. Neither the return type nor where the result goes matters, so a type parameter that no argument settles is an error, even in let xs: [int64] = empty(): cannot infer `T` in the call to `empty`; write the type arguments: `empty[T](...)`.

items.title: Explicit type arguments
items.text:
Type arguments can be written after the function's name, all of them or none:

let xs = empty[int64]()
let c = util.first[str](names)

They are spelled as for a generic struct's constructor (str, [str], int64?, Box[int64]). The wrong number is an error, and so is giving them to a function that isn't generic.

items.title: Checking
items.text:
There are no bounds on a type parameter: the body may do anything the type arguments allow, and is compiled for each instance. A signature is always checked. A body is checked only for the instances that are called, so the body of a generic function nothing calls isn't checked. An error in a body is reported once, for the first instance that hits it, and names that instance:

func largest[T](a: T, b: T) -> T {
    if a < b {               // with Color: `<` doesn't take `Color` operands; … (in `largest[Color]`)
        return b
    }
    return a
}

A generic function may call itself and other generic functions. The chain of instances has to end: one that keeps making a bigger type, like f[[T]] inside f[T], is an error once it is 64 instances deep, also when the chain runs through a generic struct's methods. A chain that branches into new types is stopped earlier, when a module passes 4096 instances.

Parameter defaults and the body resolve names in the module that wrote them, as for a generic struct's methods, and T means the instance's type in both.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A generic function is a value once it has its type arguments, as in let f = first[int64] or sorted_by(xs, less: before[T]). Without them, let f = first is an error, and they aren't inferred from where the value goes. A value's type arguments must fit on one: pair[A, B] is only read as a call, so wrap a call of it in a function literal.
  • Only top-level functions can be generic. A method can use its struct's type parameters but can't declare its own, and neither can an interface method, a function literal, an extern or main. A module-level constant can't either.
  • A function literal in a generic body can't name T, as in a generic struct's methods, because it's compiled once and not per instance.
  • A type parameter's name can't repeat in one list, and hides a type of the same name for the length of the function.

items.title: Extern functions
items.text:
