Declare external C functions with extern:

extern func labs(anon n: int64) -> int64     // compiled programs only
extern func putchar(anon c: int64) -> int64

An extern func is a C symbol, resolved at link time against the C runtime and whatever the modules of the program declare (see Link inputs): labs is in libc, and a module can name a C file of its own or a library to link. A str argument reaches C as a KodStr *, not as a char *, so a libc function that takes a C string does not fit.

items.title: Recursion
items.text:
Mutual recursion between functions is supported as long as all functions are declared in the same module.

func fib(n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n <= 1 {
        return n
    }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
}

items.title: HTTP client
items.text:
stdlib/net/http.kod makes HTTP/1.1 requests over TCP or TLS (see TCP and TLS). Its parts that don't touch the network, URLs, headers, writing a request to a Writer and reading a response from a BufReader, work on their own too.

import "net/http" { get }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let r = try get("https://example.com/")
    print(f"{r.status} {r.reason}")
    print(r.text())
    return 0
}

get, post and fetch open a connection for each request and close it afterwards (Connection: close). To make several requests over the same connection, use a Client. There is no pipelining, no cookies and no proxy support.

items.title: Requests
items.text:
A Client carries the settings that describe the service you talk to (its headers, its certificate roots, its deadline) and makes the requests:

import "net/http" { Client }
import "time" { Duration }

let client = Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15))
client.headers.add("Accept", "application/json")
client.headers.add("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)

let user = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
let made = try client.post("https://api.example.com/users", payload, content_type: "application/json")
Method of Client Meaning get(url, options = Options()), delete(url, options = Options()) GET, DELETE post(url, body, content_type, options = Options()), put(...), patch(...) the method with a bytes body and a Content-Type fetch(method, url, options = Options()) any method; the body is options.body close() close the idle connections (see Connection reuse)

All return Response or Error. The functions get, post, put, patch, delete and fetch of the module do the same with a new Client for each call, which is closed again afterwards: one request, one connection.

A Client has these fields, each with the default shown:

Field Default Meaning headers none headers sent with every request (Headers) trust_file "" PEM roots for https, as for net/tls timeout Duration(seconds: 30) limit for the connect, the TLS handshake, and each single read or write; a server that keeps sending slowly never trips it (see deadline) deadline Duration() limit for the whole request (connect, handshake, every redirect and reading the whole body); zero means none, a negative one is an InvalidInput error max_redirects 5 redirects to follow; 0 returns the redirect response as it is accept_gzip true send Accept-Encoding: gzip, and decode a gzip response (see Compression) limits see below caps on what a response may send max_idle_per_host, idle 2, Duration(seconds: 30) connection reuse (see Connection reuse)

Options is for one request. Its fields are the same, plus the body, and each one that you leave out means the Client's value:

Field Meaning headers added to the client's; where both have a header of the same name, the request's wins body the request body (bytes); empty by default trust_file, timeout, deadline, max_redirects, accept_gzip, limits replace the client's for this request, including with 0 or false 
let r = try client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration(seconds: 2)))   // this one is quicker
let q = try client.get(url, options: Options(deadline: Duration()))              // and this one has none

A Host header, Connection: close and a Content-Length (for any body, and for an empty POST, PUT or PATCH) are always set by the library and replace any you give. User-Agent: kod and Accept: */* are added when you don't give them.

URLs are http:// or https://, a host (a name, an IPv4 address, or an IPv6 address in brackets), an optional port, and an optional path and query. The scheme is case-insensitive, the default ports are 80 and 443, and a missing path is /. A fragment is dropped. Credentials in the URL (user@host), other schemes, spaces and control characters are errors.

items.title: Connection reuse
items.text:
A Client keeps the connections it has finished with and uses them again for the next request to the same scheme, host and port, which saves the TCP connect and the TLS handshake each time:

import "net/http" { Client }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let client = Client()
    let a = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
    let b = try client.get("https://api.example.com/users/2")   // same connection
    client.close()
    return 0
}

max_idle_per_host (2) is how many idle connections are kept for each scheme, host and port; 0 turns reuse off, so every request opens and closes its own. idle (30 seconds) is how old an idle connection may be before it is closed instead of reused.

A connection goes back to the Client after a response only when nothing about the exchange makes it unsafe: the response is HTTP/1.1 (or HTTP/1.0 with Connection: keep-alive), has no Connection: close, has a length (a Content-Length, chunked encoding, or no body at all, as for HEAD, 204 and 304), and left nothing unread. A response that ends where the connection ends is never reused. After any error the connection is closed.

Before an idle connection is used, the Client checks that the server has not closed it, and discards it if it has. A server can still close one in the instant between that check and the request. When a request on a reused connection then fails before any of the response arrives, and its method is GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE or TRACE (the ones that are safe to repeat), the Client makes it once more on a new connection. A POST or PATCH is not repeated, and the error is returned as it is.

Redirects use the Client too, so a redirect within one host goes over the same connection. The timeouts and the deadline apply to a reused connection exactly as to a new one. A Client is not meant to be shared by two requests at the same time, and there is only one thread.

items.title: Deadlines
items.text:
timeout bounds each wait, so a server that sends one byte every few seconds can keep a request open for as long as it likes. deadline bounds the request as a whole: the time is counted from the start of fetch and shared by every redirect, and every read and write is given only what is left of it. When it runs out the call throws an IoError of kind TimedOut whose detail is deadline exceeded, however the wait ended, and the connection is closed.

Two things can overrun it: resolving a host name is not interruptible, and a TLS connection spends up to the time left on the TCP connect and then up to the same on the handshake. Neither is by more than one timeout.

items.title: Compression
items.text:
With accept_gzip on, requests carry Accept-Encoding: gzip (unless you set an Accept-Encoding yourself), and a response whose Content-Encoding is gzip, x-gzip or deflate is decoded before you see it: Response.body holds the decoded bytes, the Content-Encoding header is removed, and Content-Length is the decoded length. This happens whenever the response says it is compressed, even from a server that was not asked to compress, and with accept_gzip off. A deflate body is meant to be zlib data, but some servers send raw deflate instead; both are read.

The decoded body is held to limits.max_body like any other, so a response that inflates past it fails with a Protocol error body too large instead of filling memory. A body that is not valid gzip is a Protocol error bad gzip body with the reason (bad deflate body for deflate), and Content-Length of the compressed data was already checked as usual. Any other Content-Encoding (br, zstd, or a list of codings) is left alone: the body comes back as received, with its header, for you to handle. A response with no body, such as one to HEAD, is not decoded.

items.title: Redirects
items.text: 301, 302 and 303 are retried as GET without a body (HEAD stays HEAD); 307 and 308 repeat the method and the body. A Location may be an absolute URL, //host/path, /path, ?query or a path relative to the request's, with . and .. segments resolved. A redirect from https to http is an error, never followed. When the redirect goes to another host or port, the Authorization, Cookie and Proxy-Authorization headers are not sent on. More than max_redirects redirects is an error.

items.title: Responses
items.text:
type Response = struct {
    status: int64
    reason: str
    headers: Headers
    body: bytes

    func text(self) -> str
    func ok(self) -> bool          // 200..299
    func header(self, anon name: str) -> str?
}

headers keeps the order the server sent and any repeated names. Headers has get(name) -> str? (the first value), all(name) -> [str], has(name), add(name, value) and set(name, value) (replaces every value of that name), and compares names without regard to case.

The body is framed as RFC 9112 says: none for HEAD, 1xx, 204 and 304; chunked when Transfer-Encoding is chunked (extensions are ignored and trailers are read and dropped); else Content-Length; else everything up to the end of the connection. 100 Continue and other 1xx responses before the real one are skipped.

Bad responses are errors, not guesses. All of these throw an IoError of kind Protocol, with op http and a detail saying what was wrong: a status line that isn't HTTP/1.x and a three-digit status, a header without a :, whitespace before the :, a header continuation line, a NUL in a header, a Content-Length that is not plain digits or that repeats with a different value, a Transfer-Encoding other than plain chunked (the client doesn't undo gzip or any other coding), a bad chunk size or a chunk without its closing line break. A connection that ends before the announced length or the last chunk is UnexpectedEof.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Limits bounds what one response may make the client read, so a hostile or broken server can't use up memory:

Field Default Exceeding it max_body 16777216 Protocol, body too large max_header_bytes 65536 Protocol, headers too large (the status line, all header lines and trailers together) max_headers 100 Protocol, too many headers

A Content-Length over max_body fails before any of the body is read.

items.title: Query strings and percent-encoding
items.text:
Put user input into a URL through Query, never by concatenating it:

import "net/http" { Query, with_query }

let q = Query()
q.add("q", "kod language")
q.add("page", "2")
let url = with_query("https://api.example.com/search", q)
// https://api.example.com/search?q=kod%20language&page=2
Function Meaning percent_encode(s) every byte except A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ becomes %XX (uppercase hex); UTF-8 text is encoded byte by byte percent_decode(s) the reverse; %XX is a byte, and + stays a +; a % not followed by two hex digits is an InvalidInput error; str or Error Query add(name, value) appends a pair, to_str() joins them as name=value&name=value, with names and values encoded; no pairs give "" with_query(url, q) url plus ? and the query, or & if url already has a ?; an empty query returns url as it is; a #fragment stays at the end

items.title: Basic authentication
items.text:
basic_auth(user, password) returns the value for an Authorization header, Basic and the base64 of user:password (RFC 7617). The text is taken as bytes, so UTF-8 passes through unchanged. A user containing : is an InvalidInput error, because the colon is what separates the two.

import "net/http" { basic_auth }

let options = Options()
options.headers.add("Authorization", try basic_auth("aladdin", "open sesame"))

items.title: Building and reading by hand
items.text:
net/http has what client is made of:

Function Meaning parse_url(s) Url or Error with scheme, host, port, target (path and query) resolve(base, location) the Url a Location points to write_request(w, req, keep_alive = false, accept_gzip = false) write a Request (method, url, headers, body) to any Writer, with Connection: close unless keep_alive, and Accept-Encoding: gzip when accept_gzip and there is no Accept-Encoding header already; header names and values with a line break or other control character, and a bad method, are InvalidInput errors read_response(br, method, limits = Limits()) read one response from a BufReader; method decides whether there is a body; Response.keep_alive says whether the connection can carry another request

write_request and read_response work on MemWriter and MemReader, which is how they are tested without a network.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• macOS on Apple Silicon (AArch64)
  • Python 3.13+
  • uv (recommended)
  • Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) — provides as and clang, which compiles the C runtime and links every program

items.title: From source
items.text:
git clone https://codeberg.org/filipsalo/kod
cd kod
uv sync

items.title: Building the self-hosted compiler
items.text:
The Makefile bootstraps everything from scratch:

make bootstrap   # clean rebuild of stage0 + stage1 (sh_kodc)
make stage1      # incremental rebuild
make test        # rebuild, then run the full test suite

uv run kod build|run|test|check runs make stage1 kod first when invoked from the repo root, so edits to the compiler, the C runtime, or the always-linked stdlib modules are picked up automatically.

items.title: Running
items.text:
kod is installed as a uv run script:

uv run kod build hello.kod   # compile to a native binary
uv run kod run hello.kod     # build + execute
uv run kod test hello.kod    # run any `test "..." {}` blocks
uv run kod check hello.kod   # parse + codegen; report errors but emit nothing

Run kod from the repository root. A global uv tool install . is not supported: the package carries no stdlib.

items.title: Linking
items.text:
link.cfg at the repository root says how programs are linked: the clang command and the C files and Kod modules every program contains. Nothing in it is specific to one machine, so most machines never touch it. One that needs something else (a Homebrew LLVM clang first on PATH that does not find the SDK, an unusual SDK) puts the names it changes in link.local.cfg next to it (only names link.cfg sets), for example:

LINK := /usr/bin/clang -target arm64-apple-darwin -Wl,-dead_strip

link.local.cfg is not tracked by git, so each new git worktree needs its own copy (cp ../link.local.cfg .). See Self-hosting for the format.

See CLI reference for the full command surface.

items.title: Streams and I/O errors
items.text:
stdlib/stream.kod defines the error type and the two interfaces that byte streams share, and stdlib/posix.kod implements them over file descriptors: files, standard input and output and, later, sockets. Code that reads or writes takes a Reader or a Writer and doesn't care what is behind it.

import "stream" { Reader, read_all }
import "posix" { open_read }

func count_bytes(anon r: Reader) -> int64 or Error {
    let data = try read_all(r)
    return len(data)
}

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let f = try open_read("data.bin")
    print_int(try count_bytes(f))
    try f.close()
    return 0
}

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Every operation that can fail returns T or Error and throws an IoError:

type IoKind = enum {
    NotFound
    PermissionDenied
    AlreadyExists
    InvalidInput
    WouldBlock      // reserved; nothing returns it yet
    TimedOut
    ConnectionRefused
    ConnectionReset
    BrokenPipe
    UnexpectedEof
    Other
    HostNotFound
    Tls
    Protocol
}

type IoError = struct {
    kind: IoKind
    op: str        // what was attempted: "open data.bin", "read", "write"
    errno: int64   // the OS error number, 0 if the error didn't come from the OS
    detail: str    // the OS's message, or a short explanation
}

to_str gives open data.bin: No such file or directory. Recover the kind with a downcast:

match open_read(path) {
    Ok(f) -> use(f)
    Err(e) ->
        if e is IoError(io) and io.kind == .NotFound {
            print("no such file")
        } else {
            print(e.to_str())
        }
}

kind_of_errno(errno) maps an OS error number to an IoKind; anything it doesn't know is Other. EAGAIN is TimedOut, because a descriptor here is only ever non-blocking through a timeout (see TCP). HostNotFound is for a name that doesn't resolve and has no OS error number (errno is 0). Tls is for a TLS failure that isn't a plain I/O error, such as a certificate that doesn't verify (see TLS). Protocol is for a peer that breaks the rules of the protocol being spoken, such as a malformed HTTP response (see HTTP). An interrupted system call is retried inside the runtime, so EINTR never reaches a caller.

items.title: Reader and Writer
items.text:
interface Reader {
    func read(self, anon max: int64) -> bytes or Error
}

interface Writer {
    func write(self, anon data: bytes) -> int64 or Error
}

read returns between 1 and max bytes, waiting until there is something to return, and returns an empty bytes at the end of the stream. With max <= 0 it returns an empty bytes without reading, so don't call it that way to test for the end. write returns how many bytes it accepted, which may be fewer than len(data); an empty data writes nothing and returns 0.

Function Meaning read_all(r) read until the end of the stream; bytes or Error read_exact(r, n) exactly n bytes, or an UnexpectedEof error; bytes or Error write_all(w, data) write every byte, repeating write as needed; a write that accepts 0 bytes of a non-empty data is an Other error (write returned 0); none or Error write_str(w, s) write_all of a str

items.title: In-memory streams
items.text: MemReader(data: bytes, pos: 0) reads from a bytes value, which is how tests and parsers get a stream without a file. MemWriter(buf: StrBuilder()) collects what is written, and to_bytes() / to_str() return a copy of it. Neither can fail.

items.title: BufReader
items.text:
BufReader wraps any Reader with a buffer, for protocols that mix lines and counted bodies such as HTTP:

let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
let status = try br.read_line()          // str?, none at the end of the stream
let body = try br.read_exact(length)     // takes what is buffered first
Method Meaning read(max) a Reader: the buffered bytes first, else one read of the inner stream read_exact(n) exactly n bytes, or UnexpectedEof read_until(delim) the bytes up to and excluding the byte delim, which is consumed; bytes?, none at the end of the stream; the last piece comes back even without a delimiter read_line() read_until(10) as a str, minus a trailing \r (str?)

Fields: inner, limit: int64 = 1048576 (a read_until or read_line longer than this fails with an InvalidInput error line too long instead of growing without bound), chunk: int64 = 8192 (the size of each inner read). ended is set when a read_until or read_line returned a last piece that the stream's end cut short, with no delimiter after it; a protocol that needs every line terminated can tell a truncation from a complete line by it. A BufReader doesn't close its inner stream.

items.title: Files and descriptors
items.text:
Fd is a file descriptor and implements both Reader and Writer:

Function Meaning open_read(path) an existing file for reading create(path) a file for writing, created (mode 0644) or truncated append(path) a file for writing, created if missing, written at its end stdin(), stdout(), stderr() descriptors 0, 1 and 2 Fd(fd: n) wrap a descriptor from elsewhere f.close() close it; none or Error f.is_terminal() whether it is a terminal, rather than a file or a pipe

stdout() writes straight to descriptor 1, bypassing the buffer that print uses. Call flush_stdout() first when you mix the two. Closing is explicit: an Fd that is dropped stays open until the program exits.

items.title: Colour
items.text:
stdlib/term.kod colours text for a terminal. term.colour(fd) says whether to: fd is a terminal, NO_COLOR is unset or empty, and TERM isn't dumb. The other functions wrap text in the escape codes of a style, whatever the output is, so check first:

import "io"
import "posix"
import "term"

func main() -> int64 {
    mut label = "error:"
    if term.colour(posix.stderr()) {
        label = term.red(term.bold(label))
    }
    io.write_stderr(f"{label} no such file\n")
    return 1
}

The styles are bold, dim, red, green and yellow.

The older io.read_file and io.write_file keep their behavior: an empty string or -1 on failure, with no reason.

items.title: TCP
items.text:
stdlib/net/tcp.kod opens TCP connections. A connection is an Fd, so it is a Reader and a Writer and works with BufReader, read_all and the rest. A program that imports it compiles and links stdlib/net/tcp.c; no other program does.

import "net/tcp" { connect, set_timeout }
import "time" { Duration }
import "stream" { BufReader, write_str }

func fetch_status_line(host: str) -> str or Error {
    let conn = try connect(host, port: 80)
    try set_timeout(conn, timeout: Duration(seconds: 5))
    try write_str(conn, "HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n")
    let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
    let line = try br.read_line()
    try conn.close()
    return line? or ""
}
Function Meaning connect(host, port, timeout = Duration(seconds: 10)) resolve host (a name or an IP literal, IPv4 or IPv6) and connect to the first address that answers; Fd or Error set_timeout(f, timeout) make a read or a write on f fail with TimedOut after a Duration without progress; zero means wait forever; none or Error listen(host, port, backlog = 128) a Listener bound to host:port; an empty host means every IPv4 interface and port 0 picks a free port; Listener or Error l.accept() the next connection, waiting for one; Fd or Error is_idle(f) true if nothing is waiting to be read from f; false if it has data, an end of stream (the peer closed it) or an error pending l.port() the port it is bound to l.close() stop listening; none or Error

connect gives up on each address after timeout, so a host with several unreachable addresses can take longer in all. A refused connection is ConnectionRefused, a timeout TimedOut, a name that doesn't resolve HostNotFound, and a port outside 0..65535 or an empty host InvalidInput. Writing to a peer that has closed is a BrokenPipe error and doesn't kill the program with SIGPIPE. A connection has TCP_NODELAY set.

items.title: TLS
items.text:
stdlib/net/tls.kod runs TLS over a TCP connection, using the system's SecureTransport (the Security framework), so it needs nothing installed and checks certificates against the macOS keychain. A program that imports it links -framework Security -framework CoreFoundation; no other program does.

import "net/tls" { connect }
import "stream" { BufReader, write_str }

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let conn = try connect("example.com", port: 443)
    try write_str(conn, "GET / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n")
    let br = BufReader(inner: conn)
    print((try br.read_line())? or "")
    try conn.close()
    return 0
}

A TlsStream is a Reader and a Writer, so everything above works on it as on a plain connection.

Function Meaning connect(host, port, trust_file = "", timeout = Duration(seconds: 10)) open a TCP connection with net/tcp and run the TLS handshake; TlsStream or Error s.read(max), s.write(data) as for any stream s.set_timeout(timeout) as net/tcp.set_timeout: a read or write fails with TimedOut after a Duration without progress s.close() send a close notice, then close the connection; none or Error

The server's certificate must be valid for host, chain to a trusted root and be in date; otherwise connect throws an IoError of kind Tls whose detail says why, and the connection is closed. timeout limits the TCP connect and, separately, the handshake. A server that can't speak TLS 1.2 is a Tls error: SecureTransport has no TLS 1.3, and the minimum version is 1.2.

trust_file is the path of a PEM file of certificates. When it isn't empty, those certificates are the only trusted roots, in place of the keychain: use it for a private CA or a self-signed server. The host name is still checked.

A server that closes the connection without a close notice reads as an ordinary end of stream, since plain HTTP/1.0 servers do that; a response that carries its own length (Content-Length or chunked) shows a truncation anyway.

items.title: JSON
items.text: stdlib/json.kod parses and emits JSON, strictly as RFC 8259 defines it.

items.title: Quick example
items.text:
import "json"

func main() -> int64 or Error {
    let v = try json.parse("{\"name\": \"kod\", \"tags\": [1, 2.5, \"\\u00e9\"]}")
    let name = v.get("name").as_str()
    print(name? or "?")                       // kod
    print(v.emit())                           // {"name":"kod","tags":[1,2.5,"é"]}
    print(v.emit_pretty())
    return 0
}

items.title: Parsing
items.text:
func parse(anon src: str, max_depth: int64 = 512) -> Value or Error

Malformed input is an error you can handle, never a panic. The error is a JsonError, which carries where it went wrong:

type JsonError = struct {
    message: str     // "unexpected character", "unterminated string", ...
    offset: int64    // byte offset in the input
    line: int64      // 1-based
    column: int64    // 1-based, in bytes
}

Its to_str reads json: unexpected character at line 2, column 7. Recover it with a downcast (e is JsonError(je), see Types).

What the parser accepts is exactly JSON text: one value, with optional whitespace (space, tab, newline, carriage return) around it. It rejects, with an error saying what and where:

  • an empty input, text after the value, and a missing or doubled comma, colon or bracket;
  • trailing commas, comments, single quotes, unquoted keys, NaN, Infinity and a leading +;
  • numbers like 01, -, 1., .5, 1e and 0x10;
  • a raw control character (below U+0020) inside a string;
  • an escape other than \" \\ \/ \b \f \n \r \t \uXXXX;
  • a \u escape that isn't four hex digits, and an unpaired surrogate (\ud800 not followed by \udc00..\udfff, or a lone low surrogate);
  • nesting deeper than max_depth, which stops [[[[... from exhausting the stack. Depth counts the arrays and objects around a value, so max_depth: 1 allows [1] and not [[1]].

A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start is skipped. Bytes of 0x80 and up inside strings are taken as they are: the parser doesn't check that they are valid UTF-8.

items.title: The Value type
items.text:
type Value = enum {
    Null
    Bool(value: bool)
    Number(value: int64)
    Str(value: str)
    Array(items: [Value])
    Object(keys: [str], values: [Value])
    Decimal(text: str)
}

An integer that fits in int64 is a Number (-0 is Number(0)). Any other number is a Decimal: one with a fraction or an exponent (2.5, 1e3, -0.0), or an integer too large for int64. A Decimal keeps the number's text exactly as it was written, so nothing is rounded and it is written back unchanged. Read it as a float64 with parse_float on as_number_text(), and build one with to_str. \uXXXX escapes are decoded into UTF-8, with a surrogate pair giving one four-byte character, and \u0000 gives a NUL byte inside the str.

Object entries are stored as parallel arrays (keys[i] is the key of values[i]), in the order they were written. A repeated key is kept, and get finds the first.

items.title: Accessors
items.text:
Methods on Value. None of them can fail: they return Null or none when the value isn't what you asked for, so v.get("a").get("b") is safe on any input.

Method Returns v.get(key) the first value of that key in an object; Null if the key is missing or v isn't an object v.at(index) the element of an array; Null if out of range or v isn't an array v.as_str() str?, for a Str v.as_int() int64?, for a Number (a Decimal is none, even 3.0) v.as_bool() bool?, for a Bool v.as_array() [Value]?, for an Array v.as_number_text() str?, the text of a Number or a Decimal v.is_null() bool

items.title: Building values
items.text:
Constructing a Value by hand means .Object(keys: [...], values: [...]) with two arrays that must stay in step. Two builders do the bookkeeping:

let body = json.ObjectBuilder()
body.put_str("title", "a bug")
body.put_int("priority", 2)
body.put_bool("urgent", false)
body.put("labels", json.array_of([.Str(value: "bug"), .Str(value: "ui")]))
let text = body.build().emit()
// {"title":"a bug","priority":2,"urgent":false,"labels":["bug","ui"]}
Method Meaning put(key, value) add an entry with any Value; entries keep the order they were added in, and a repeated key is added again put_str(key, s), put_int(key, n), put_bool(key, b), put_null(key) the same for the common cases build() -> Value the Object; the builder can go on being used

array_of(items: Items) -> Value makes an Array from a [Value]; str_value(s), int_value(n) and bool_value(b) make the scalar Values, for building those arrays.

items.title: Emitting
items.text:
func emit(self) -> str
func emit_pretty(self, indent: int64 = 2) -> str

Both are methods on Value: v.emit(), v.emit_pretty(indent: 4).

emit writes compact JSON with no spaces. emit_pretty puts each array element and object entry on its own line, indented by indent spaces per level, with ": " after a key; an empty array or object is [] or {}, and there is no newline at the end. Both write strings with \", \\, \b, \f, \n, \r, \t and \u00XX for any other control character, and leave everything else, UTF-8 included, as it is. The text of a Decimal is written verbatim; a Decimal built by hand whose text isn't a JSON number is written as null, so the output is always valid JSON.

Emitting what parse(s) returns gives the same JSON as s, except for the whitespace, the choice of escapes in strings, and -0 written as 0.

items.title: Memory Layout
items.text: This document describes how Kod values are represented in memory at runtime.

items.title: Primitive types
items.text:
Primitive values are stored directly — on the stack in local variables, or passed by value in registers.

Type Width Representation int64 8 Two's-complement 64-bit int float64 8 IEEE 754 binary64 bit pattern, in an integer slot str 8 Pointer to null-terminated C string in .data section bool 1 0 (false) or 1 (true) none 8 Always 0 (null sentinel)

items.title: Struct values
items.text:
Struct variables are reference types: the variable holds an 8-byte pointer to the struct's data, which lives on the heap.

stack slot (8 bytes)          heap memory
┌──────────────┐              ┌──────────────┐
│   pointer ───┼─────────────▶│   field 0    │  offset 0
└──────────────┘              │   field 1    │  offset 8
                              │   ...        │
                              └──────────────┘

Fields are laid out sequentially in declaration order, each at its natural alignment. The total allocation size (data_width) is the sum of all field widths.

items.title: Example: Point
items.text:
type Point = struct {
    x: int64    // offset 0, width 8
    y: int64    // offset 8, width 8
}
  • data_width = 16 (allocated on the heap)
  • width = 8 (size of the pointer stored in a stack slot)

items.title: Reference semantics
items.text:
Assigning a struct variable copies the pointer, not the data:

let p = Point(x: 3, y: 4)
let q: Point = p        // q and p point to the same object
q.x = 10               // also modifies p.x

The same holds for any expression that yields a struct, such as a call, a match expression, x? or fallback or try f(): the binding stores the pointer the expression produced.

items.title: Enum values
items.text:
Enums are heap-allocated, like structs. A stack slot holds an 8-byte pointer; the cell at the pointer is:

[offset 0]  discriminant : int64  (variant index starting from 1)
[offset 8]  payload      : max(variant payload sizes) bytes

Because enum variables are pointers, they fit in a single register and pass through the ARM64 calling convention without any multi-word ABI gymnastics.

See docs/enums.md for details.

items.title: Union values
items.text: A union is an enum the compiler writes, with one variant per member, so its value is a pointer to a cell of the same shape: the discriminant says which member it holds, and the payload is that member's 8-byte value. Members are numbered in a fixed order worked out from the types themselves, so a union is laid out the same in every module however it's spelled. A struct, enum or other reference held in a union is a pointer to its own cell, so it costs a second allocation. A T | none is a T? with an optional's layout; the optional of a larger union is an optional cell holding a pointer to a union cell.

items.title: Reclaiming memory
items.text:
Kod counts references. Every struct, enum value, optional cell, interface cell, array and computed string has a count, and it is freed when the count reaches 0, as are the references it held. A program does nothing to make this happen: there is no free, no scope to declare and no collector that pauses it, and a server that handles requests for days stays the size its live data needs.

A cycle is never freed. Two values that refer to each other keep each other alive after the last outside reference is gone:

type Node = struct {
    name: str
    other: Node?
}

let a = Node(name: "a", other: none)
let b = Node(name: "b", other: a)
a.other = b  // a and b now live until the program exits

A closure makes a cycle easy to write without seeing it: a closure stored in a struct it captures keeps that struct alive, as in req.on_done = func() { req.count += 1 }. That costs nothing for something that lives as long as the program, and leaks once per req for something made per request.

For a long-running program, break the cycle when you are done with it (a.other = none), or keep the back reference as an index or a key instead of a struct. Most data, including all of the compiler's, has no cycles.

Memory that has been freed is used again for new values but isn't returned to the OS, so a program stays as big as it has ever been. There are no threads, so counts aren't atomic.

items.title: The heap
items.text:
Counted objects live in one reserved address range of 64 GB (stdlib/rc.c), so whether a pointer is counted is a check on its address, and string literals and vtables need no count. A program that fills the range stops with rc: the counted heap is full.

The 8 bytes before an object hold its header:

[offset -8]  count      : 32 bits
[offset -4]  size class :  8 bits
[offset -3]  slot mask  : 24 bits
[offset  0]  the object

Bits 0 to 20 of the mask say which 8-byte slots of the object hold references, which is what freeing follows. Bit 21 marks an array whose elements are references, bit 22 an array, and bit 23 an object with references past slot 20, whose block ends in a pointer to a descriptor of them in the data section.

A block comes from the free list of its size class, or else from the end of the used part of the range. Classes go up in steps of 16 bytes to 1 KB and in powers of two after that.

items.title: What generated code does
items.text:
• A call returns a reference its caller owns. A value a statement computes and doesn't keep is released when the statement ends.
  • A store into a variable, field or element retains the new value and releases the old one. When the value is fresh the store takes the reference over instead.
  • A function borrows its parameters: a parameter costs nothing unless the body assigns to it. So that what it borrows can't go away, a caller holds a value it read from a field or element for the length of the statement.
  • A function releases its variables when it returns.

retain and release are calls with the object in x17, to _rc_retain_stub and _rc_release_stub. They change only x16, x17 and lr, and no flags, until an object is freed, and freeing saves the rest, so they can sit anywhere in an expression.

items.title: Function values
items.text:
A function value is a reference to a cell whose first word is the address of the code. A named function or a literal that captures nothing has one such cell in the data section, written only if the function is used as a value, and using it never allocates. A literal that captures allocates a counted cell each time it's evaluated, with the captured values after the code address:

closure cell:  [code, capture 0, capture 1, ...]

A call through a function value is ldr x16, [f]; mov x17, f; blr x16, so a function reached that way finds its cell in x17. One that captures copies the values into its frame on entry and borrows them, like parameters, since its caller keeps the cell alive for the call. Other functions ignore x17.

A mut that a literal captures is kept in a counted one-word struct from its declaration on (_MutCell[T] in builtins.kod). The function's slot and each closure that captures it hold a reference to the struct, and a read or an assignment loads or stores its word. The parser makes the change, so codegen sees an ordinary let of a struct and n.value for each use of n.

items.title: Testing for mistakes
items.text:
To test the rules themselves, build the runtime so that freed memory is overwritten and never used again, by putting this in link.local.cfg and running the tests:

CFLAGS := -target arm64-apple-darwin -I stdlib -O2 -DRC_POISON

A use after free then shows as wrong output or a crash. -DRC_STATS adds counts of allocations and frees, printed at exit when KOD_RC_STATS is set. A program can declare extern func rc_live_bytes() -> int64 to ask how much of the heap is in use.

items.title: Calling convention (ARM64, macOS)
items.text:
• Arguments: passed in x0–x7
  • Return value: in x0
  • Caller-saved: x0–x15
  • Callee-saved: x19–x28
  • Frame pointer: fp (x29)
  • Link register: lr (x30)

Since struct variables are 8-byte pointers, they fit in a single register and can be passed to and returned from functions normally.

items.title: Stack frame
items.text: A function pushes fp and lr, points fp at them and keeps each local in an 8-byte slot below fp, including the compiler's own temporaries. Values that must survive a call in the middle of an expression are pushed below those slots. The epilogue restores sp from fp, so a try that returns from inside an expression, such as an array literal element or a call argument, leaves the stack as the function found it.

items.title: Modules
items.text: Each .kod file is a module. Imports name either a file relative to the importing module or a stdlib module.

items.title: Importing
items.text:
Two forms:

import "./utils"        // relative — utils.kod next to the importing file
import "./math/vec"     // relative — math/vec.kod below the importing file's directory
import "kod/ast"        // stdlib — stdlib/kod/ast.kod
import "io"             // stdlib — stdlib/io.kod

Paths beginning with ./ resolve against the directory of the importing file, not the project root or the current directory. Anything else resolves under stdlib/.

The imported module's public names are accessible via the import alias, which is the last path component:

import "./math/vec"

func origin() -> vec.Vec2 {
    return vec.Vec2(x: 0, y: 0)
}

Qualified constructors have the imported type, so let v = vec.Vec2(x: 1, y: 2) needs no annotation before v.x. Calling a function the module doesn't declare, such as vec.lenght(v), is an error with a did-you-mean hint. No local can be named like an import alias: a let, mut, parameter, for variable or pattern binding named vec is an error, `vec` is the name of an import; give the local another name, so vec. always means the module. A function named like an import alias doesn't hide it: with func vec() declared too, vec() calls the function and vec.make(1) the module's.

To use some names unqualified instead, list them after the path:

import "./math/vec" { Vec2, dot }

func norm2(anon v: Vec2) -> int64 {
    return dot(v, v)
}

An import that lists names binds only those names, not its alias, so vec.dot is an error there (unknown name `vec`; an import that lists names binds no `vec`, so add a plain import of it to write `vec.`) and a local may be named vec. That keeps the usual way of naming a value after its module working:

import "net/http" { Client }

let client = Client()      // `client` is a local, and `http` names nothing

To have both, import the module twice: import "./math/vec" binds vec and import "./math/vec" { Vec2 } adds Vec2, and then no local can be named vec.

Each listed name must be a function, extern, constant, variable or type the module declares; otherwise it's an error with a did-you-mean hint: module `vec` has no function, constant or type `dto`; did you mean `dot`?.

items.title: Where names resolve
items.text:
Parameter defaults, struct field defaults and the method bodies of a generic type resolve function names, type names and import aliases in the module that wrote them, even though they run as part of the caller's code. A default in util.kod that calls helper() calls util's own helper, a function util imports with { helper }, or the builtin of that name, never one that belongs to the caller. Likewise rng.seed() in that default means util's own import "./rng", whether or not the caller imports a module named rng:

// util.kod
func helper() -> int64 {
    return 1
}

func f(x: int64 = helper()) -> int64 {
    return x
}

// main.kod
import "./util"

func helper() -> int64 {
    return 2
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let helper = 3          // not visible to util's default either
    print(f"{util.f()}")    // 1
    return 0
}

The same holds for a function literal or a function value used as a default (cb: func() -> int64 = helper). A name the defining module doesn't have is an error, reported at the default when a call leaves the parameter out, even when the caller happens to declare it.

A bare type name T means, in this order: a type parameter of the generic declaration around it, a primitive (int64, bool, str, bytes, none), a type the module declares (its own aliases included), a type it lists in an import (import "./pa" { Pt }), then a builtin type. A type of a module imported without listing it, or loaded only because another module imports it, is written through the module: pa.Pt. Otherwise it's an error with a hint naming the file that declares it: unknown type `Pt`; lib/pa.kod declares `Pt`: write `pa.Pt` or list it in the import (`{ Pt }`), or unknown type `Pt`; lib/pa.kod declares `Pt`: import it to use it here when the module doesn't import that file. kod finds the file anywhere in the program being built, so the hint also names a module that imports this one or that only another module imports. sh_kodc run on one file knows only that file's imports.

m.T means a type that the module imported as m declares, its own aliases included. This holds in a type, a constructor m.T(...), a type argument, m.E.V and a pattern b: m.T. Types that m only imports aren't reachable through it. Otherwise it's an error: module `m` has no type `T`, with a did-you-mean over m's types (module `m` has no function or type `T` for a call m.T(...)). When m isn't a module this one imports, the error spells what was written: unknown type `m.T`. A generic type takes its arguments the same way, as in m.Box[m.Pt](v: p), also where it is itself a type argument: Stack[m.Box[str]].

A module exports only what it declares, never what it imports. When m lists T in one of its own imports, m.T, m.f(), m.f and import "./m" { T } say where T comes from: `T` is imported by `m`, not declared there; import it from lib/b.kod. A value of such a type can still be used without naming it, as in let t = m.make(). To pass a type on deliberately, m declares an alias of it, type T = b.T (which needs a plain import "./b"), and for a function a wrapper.

A module declares each of its names once. A function, extern, struct, enum, interface or type alias with the name of an earlier one in the same module is an error at the second declaration (`f` is already declared on line 1), and so is a method, field or variant with the name of an earlier one of the same struct, interface or enum (`Kind.A` is already declared on line 2). A method can't take the name of a field of its struct either; the error is at the method (`Bag.len` is already declared on line 3).

A name an import lists counts the same way. A module can't both declare a name and list it in an import, and two imports can't list the same name, whether it names a type or a function. The later one is the error: `Pt` is already imported on line 1, or `Pt` is already declared on line 3 when the declaration comes first. Two imports can't share a name either, unless they load the same file: after import "./a/util", import "./b/util" is `util` is already imported on line 1, while a second import "./a/util" { Vec2 } only adds to the first import's list.

Each module's structs, enums, interfaces and type aliases are its own. Two modules may declare a type of the same name, and they are different types: pa.Pt and pb.Pt don't convert to each other, is pa.Pt doesn't hold for a pb.Pt, and Box[pa.Pt] and Box[pb.Pt] are different instances. Aliases of different types may share a name across modules, and an alias may take its target's name (type Pt = pb.Pt), so a module that imports only this one reaches the type as its Pt. Only the builtins may declare Map, Option, Result, Error, Stringable or ExitCode; anywhere else it's an error: `Option` is the name of a builtin type; give this type another name. A module is one module however its path is spelled: import "./lib/../lib/pa" and import "./lib/pa" load the same file once.

A message writes a type by its bare name, unless another module of the program declares a struct, enum or interface of that name too (an alias doesn't count, as a message writes the type it stands for). Then it's written the way the module being compiled would write it (pa.Pt, or Pt when the module has it under that name: declared, aliased or listed in an import), or with its file when that module can't name it (Pt (lib/pb.kod)).

items.title: Standard library
items.text:
The stdlib lives under stdlib/ in the repository.

Module Contents builtins Always imported. print, print_int, len, fail, Map[K, V], the Error / Stringable / ExitCode interfaces. primitives/int64, primitives/float64, primitives/str, primitives/bool (and int64_float, str_float, which hold to_float64 and parse_float, and float_text, which both float methods use) Methods on the primitive types (to_str, hash, parse_float). Auto-loaded; not imported directly. io read_file, write_file, and stdin/stdout/stderr helpers. fs FileSystem interface with DiskFs (real disk) and MemFs (in-memory, for tests). process process.run(argv) — spawn a subprocess and capture stdout/stderr/exit code. process.exec(argv) — replace the calling process (compiled programs only). env get, set and unset for environment variables. See Built-ins. time monotonic_ns(), unix_ns(), Duration, sleep(d), and Time with now(), parse(s) and parse_date(s). See Time. sets Set[T], a hash set built on Map: Set[str](), with add, contains, remove(x) -> bool, values() and len; for x in s goes over the elements in the order they were first added. sort sorted(xs) and sorted_by(xs, less:), stable, returning a new array. See Arrays. arrays contains(xs, x) and equal(a, b). See Arrays. json Strict JSON parse/emit, with builders. See JSON. strbuilder, stream, posix StrBuilder; Reader / Writer and IoError; file descriptors. See Strings and Streams. net/tcp, net/tls, net/http TCP, TLS, and HTTP/1.1 messages with a client. See Streams and HTTP client. jsonrpc Content-Length framed messages on stdin/stdout, as used by LSP. encoding/base64 Base64, standard and URL-safe, strict decoding. See Encodings. hash/crc32 CRC-32 (gzip polynomial), streaming or one-shot. compress/deflate, compress/inflate Compress to and decompress from gzip, zlib and raw deflate. See Encodings. kod/ast AST node types (for the self-hosted compiler). kod/lexing Tokenizer (self-hosted). kod/parsing Parser (self-hosted). kod/codegen ARM64 code generator.

items.title: Circular imports
items.text: Circular imports work: a struct, enum or interface declared in a module of the cycle is the same type on either side, so a value of it can be passed both ways, also inside an array, an optional, a Map or another generic type's instance such as Box[Pt], and is recovers a struct from an interface value whichever side boxed it.

items.title: Visibility
items.text:
Top-level functions, externs, constants and types are visible to importing modules, except those whose name starts with _. Those are private to the module that declares them, which uses them like any other name:

// lib.kod
let _LIMIT: int64 = 3

type _Slot = struct {
    n: int64
}

func _clamp(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    if n > _LIMIT {
        return _LIMIT
    }
    return n
}

func slots(anon n: int64) -> int64 {
    return _Slot(n: _clamp(n)).n
}

// main.kod
import "./lib"

func main() -> int64 {
    print_int(lib.slots(5))     // 3
    lib._clamp(5)               // error: `_clamp` is private to module `lib`
    return 0
}

The same error is reported for lib._LIMIT, lib._Slot(...), lib._Slot in a type, and _clamp in an import list (import "./lib" { _clamp }). Did-you-mean hints never suggest another module's private names.

A private name keeps a helper out of the module's interface, so the module can change or remove it without breaking its importers. A public function may still take or return a private type: callers can use such a value, its fields and its methods, but can't write the type's name. Fields and methods whose names start with _ are private to their struct; see Structs.

A module's top level holds declarations (func, type, interface, import, extern and test) constants (let NAME: T = value, see Module-level constants) and variables (mut NAME: T = value, see Module-level variables). Any statement there is an error. Constants and variables are visible to importing modules like functions, and only the declaring module assigns a variable.

items.title: Symbol and object names
items.text:
A module is identified by its normalized path: ./x and ./a/../x are one module, while x (the file under stdlib/) and ./x (the project's own) are two. Everything a module emits (functions, types, tests) is labelled $<prefix>$<name>. The prefix is computed from the path and from whether stdlib/<path>.kod exists (step 5):

  1. Drop the .kod extension, and the leading / of an absolute path.
  2. A path under stdlib/ drops that directory: stdlib/io.kod is io, stdlib/kod/ast.kod is kod$ast.
  3. Each remaining byte becomes symbol characters. / becomes $. Letters, digits and _ stay. . stays, except as the first byte. Every other byte (space, -, +, @, $, each byte of a non-ASCII character) becomes $$ followed by its two lowercase hex digits: my-app is my$$2dapp.
  4. The label is $<prefix>$<name>, and the assembler reads $ followed by a digit as a number, and takes no $$name at all, so a prefix is never empty and never starts with $ or a digit. If it would, a . is put in front: -x is .$$2dx, 01_hello is .01_hello, 2024/report is .2024$report, and a file named .kod is .. (A digit after an inner $ is fine: tests/3d is tests$3d.) The assembler also reads . and digits followed by e or E as a number (.1e5), so then that letter is written $$65 or $$45 as well: 1e5 is .1$$655, 2East/lib is .2$$45ast$lib.
  5. A module outside stdlib/ whose path also exists under stdlib/ is in the namespace .user$: a project's io.kod is .user$io and does not clash with the stdlib io. The check is a file test, so on a case-insensitive volume a project's Io.kod also gets the marker; that is harmless, because every project module is recompiled for each program.

Two different normalized paths never get the same prefix: a prefix's own leading . is always escaped by step 3, so a raw leading . comes only from step 4, the marker .user$ starts .u, which step 4 never produces, and $$65 and $$45 are escapes that step 3 never writes (it keeps letters). (An absolute path and the relative path with the same components still collide, as before.)

A vtable and a type's identity word are shared between objects by label, so their labels have to differ for different types as well: the parts of those labels are joined with $$for$, $$of$ and the like, which step 3 never writes (a $$ it writes has two hex digits after it). is and interface calls therefore can't mix up two types, whatever their paths are called. A method's label joins its type and name the same way, $<prefix>$<Type>$$m$<name>, so T.m in x.kod and a function m in x/T.kod are two symbols, not one defined twice.

kod build writes a program's objects under build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/, mirroring the source tree: stdlib/json.kod becomes <stem>.obj/stdlib/json.kod.o, a project's lib/json.kod becomes <stem>.obj/lib/json.kod.o; the assembly .s sits beside each .o. A .. directory is written %2e%2e (a . one %2e), the root of an absolute path %2f, and a literal % in a name %25. The _main shim is <stem>.obj/<entry>.main.{s,o} (<stem>.obj/<first entry>.testmain.{s,o} for tests). The executable is build/apps/<stem>/<stem>, or <stem>_test for kod test; <stem>.obj can equal neither. <stem> is the entry's file name without .kod; for kod test <dir> it is the directory with every byte outside letters, digits, _ and - replaced by _ (its last 200 bytes, when it is longer), then _tests. A file whose name without .kod is empty, . or .. (.kod, ..kod, ...kod) has no program name and is refused. An entry named kod or lsp (other than tools/kod.kod and tools/lsp.kod, however they are spelled) is refused, because its executable would replace the tool. So is one whose directory the volume takes for the tool's, such as KOD on a case-insensitive volume.

The object path has to fit the file system as well: a file name of more than about 240 bytes (the shim adds .kod.main.s), or an absolute entry path of more than about 950 bytes (build/apps/<stem>/<stem>.obj/%2f/ goes in front of it), is too long, and the build stops with a message that a file could not be opened or a directory made.

kod test <dir> builds every *_test.kod below <dir> into one program, except a file with a path component below <dir> that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files, the scratch .kod_compile_test.kod) and a build directory directly below <dir>. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.

items.title: Link inputs
items.text:
A module that needs C code or a system library says so in the comment lines at the top of its file, before its first declaration:

// kod:require ${OPENSSL}/include/openssl/ssl.h  brew install openssl@3
// kod:cc tls.c -I${OPENSSL}/include
// kod:link -L${OPENSSL}/lib -lssl -lcrypto

import "io"
  • kod:cc <file.c> [flags...]: a C file beside the module. kod build compiles it with CC and CFLAGS of link.cfg followed by the flags given, and links the object. Flags are passed as written; a relative -I is relative to the repository root, where kod runs. The file is compiled on every build, like the modules, so an edit to it, to a header it includes or to CC and CFLAGS is picked up by the next one. A C file that several modules of a program name (or several test files of one kod test <dir>) is compiled and linked once; naming it with different flags is an error.
  • kod:link <args...>: arguments for the final link, after all objects: -lz, -L..., -framework Security, a path to a .a. They are passed in the order the modules appear in the program, and a -lname that comes up again is passed once.
  • kod:require <file> [hint...]: the file (a path from the repository root, or an absolute one) must exist before anything is compiled; otherwise the build stops with path:line:1: error: needs <file> (<hint>) (needs <file> when there is no hint), for each such file, naming the line of the directive. Use it for a file outside the repository that the other lines rely on, so that a machine without it gets the hint instead of 'openssl/err.h' file not found.

${NAME} in a word is replaced by the value of NAME in link.cfg, or in link.local.cfg when that overrides it (the example assumes link.cfg has an OPENSSL line). A name that neither file sets, or one whose value is not exactly one word, is an error, and so is a $ that does not start ${NAME}. Words are separated by spaces; there is no quoting, and a tab or another control character in a directive line is an error.

Only the leading block counts: the lines from the top of the file that are blank or start with //, up to the first other line. In it a line that starts with // kod: (after any indent) is a directive, and any other comment line is just a comment; a // kod: line further down is a comment too and does nothing. A line in the block that is spelled like a directive but not so (//kod:cc x.c, // kod:cc x.c, // Kod:cc x.c, // kod :cc x.c) is an error, so that a slip is not taken for a comment. A UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of the file is skipped, as the compiler skips it. Put a blank line after the block, or the first declaration takes it as its doc comment (shown on hover).

These are errors, path:line:1: error: ..., from kod build, kod run, kod test and kod check: an unknown directive (unknown directive kod:linkk), a directive spelled almost right, a tab in a directive line, a directive without its argument, a kod:cc that does not name a .c file beside the module (a bare file name ending in .c, which has to exist), and a ${NAME} that cannot be replaced. kod check validates the lines, and that the C file is there, but it does not test kod:require and compiles no C.

Only a program that imports the module compiles its C file or passes its arguments, and that includes a module that only a test file imports: kod test reads the lines of every module of its program, and kod test <dir> builds all its files into one program, so one test file's missing kod:require file stops them all. A program that imports no such module compiles no C file. A C file's object is <stem>.obj/<path>.c.o in the tree of Symbol and object names, next to the module's own <path>.kod.o. If the C compiler fails, kod shows its output and kod: compiling <file> failed, exits 1 and links nothing.

A module that declares link inputs cannot be one that the Makefile builds: it does not read their lines. That is a module listed in STAGE0_KOD of link.cfg, one of the compiler's own modules (COMPILER_KOD in the Makefile) and kodc.kod and tools/kod.kod. For a STAGE0_KOD module the driver says so (path:line:1: error: ...) and stops, rather than leave the lines unread; for the others a test of the repository checks that there are none.

C files export bare symbols into one namespace shared with libc and runtime.c: name them kod_<module>_.... #include "kod_rt.h" (CFLAGS has -I stdlib) declares what they need of the runtime:

  • KodStr: what a Kod str is when it crosses into C. buf points at len bytes followed by a NUL byte, and a str parameter or result is a KodStr *.
  • KodArray: a Kod [T]: ptr points at len 8-byte slots, with room for cap.
  • arena_alloc(size): memory that is never freed.
  • rc_alloc(size, mask): a counted object, zeroed, with a count of 1 that the caller owns. mask says which of its 8-byte slots hold references, bit 0 for the first; it must not use bits past 20. rc_alloc_raw is the same but leaves filling it to the caller. rc_retain_c(p) and rc_release_c(p) count a reference up and down, and do nothing for memory outside the counted heap.
  • kod_str_new(len): a new str of len bytes for the caller to fill in. kod_str_from_bytes(p, n): a str that is a copy of n bytes at p, which may contain NUL bytes.
  • panic(msg): print panic: and the message with a backtrace, and exit 1.

A function value isn't a C function pointer, so an extern can't take or return one: an `extern` can't take or return a function value.

Kod values are reference counted, and C code follows the same rules as generated code. A parameter is borrowed: it stays alive during the call, and C code that keeps it after returning calls rc_retain_c. A result is owned by the caller, which releases it, so returning anything other than a new object, such as a parameter or something kept in a static, takes an rc_retain_c first. The same goes for references written into an object: each one needs its own count.

items.title: Pattern matching
items.text: Kod's match statement dispatches on a value and binds sub-parts.

items.title: Syntax
items.text:
match <expression> {
    <pattern> -> <arm-body>
    <pattern> -> {
        // multi-statement arm
    }
}

Arms are tested top-to-bottom. The first matching arm executes.

items.title: Catch-all (else)
items.text:
else matches any value the other arms didn't cover. It must be the last arm. The arrow is optional after else:

match x {
    1    -> print("one")
    2    -> print("two")
    else -> print("other")    // arrow form
}

match x {
    1 -> print("one")
    else { print("other") }   // block form
}

items.title: Integer literal
items.text:
match n {
    0    -> print("zero")
    1    -> print("one")
    -1   -> print("minus one")
    else -> print("other")
}

A - directly before the digits makes the literal negative. As in an expression, the smallest int64 is written -9223372036854775808. Only a literal can be a pattern, so -n is not one.

items.title: String literal
items.text:
match s {
    "hello" -> print("greeting")
    "bye"   -> print("farewell")
    else    -> print("unknown")
}

items.title: Bool
items.text:
match b {
    true  -> print("yes")
    false -> print("no")
}

A literal pattern needs a value of its own type, so matching a str against 3 is an error. On an optional it tests the value inside (see Optional): 3 on an int64? matches a 3 and not none.

items.title: Enum variant (explicit)
items.text:
type Color = enum {
    Red
    Green
    Blue
}

match c {
    Color.Red   -> print("red")
    Color.Green -> print("green")
    Color.Blue  -> print("blue")
}

items.title: Enum variant (implicit shorthand)
items.text:
When the type is clear from context, the enum name can be omitted:

match c {
    .Red   -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
    .Blue  -> print("blue")
}

items.title: Payload variant
items.text:
Bind the payload fields:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

match shape {
    Shape.Circle(radius) -> print_int(radius)
    Shape.Rect(w, h)     -> print_int(w * h)
}

Bindings are by position — the names in the pattern don't have to match the field names. A pattern may bind fewer names than the variant has fields, but not more, and it can't bind one name twice, though _ and _name can repeat. Naming an enum or variant that doesn't exist is an error, as is an implicit .Variant that no enum declares.

Each binding takes the type of the field it binds, so different arms can reuse a name for payloads of different types:

type Value = enum {
    I(value: int64)
    S(value: str)
}

match v {
    .I(value) -> print(f"int {value}")
    .S(value) -> print(f"str {value}")
}

items.title: Optional
items.text:
match maybe_n {
    Some(n) -> print_int(n)
    none    -> print("nothing")
}

A pattern that can't match none (a literal, a variant or a type pattern) tests the value inside, so it needs no Some. _, and a name in a payload position, match the optional itself, none included, so Some(n) is how to bind what's inside:

let color: Color? = .Red
match color {
    .Red    -> print("red")
    .Rgb(v) -> print_int(v)
    none    -> print("no color")
}

let count: int64? = 0
match count {
    0    -> print("zero")
    none -> print("unknown")
    else -> print("some")
}

The same holds inside another pattern and after is: color is .Red is false for none.

items.title: Type patterns
items.text:
A union is an enum whose variants are named by their types. T(name) matches when the value holds a T, and binds it as a T; a bare T only tests. none is the member that holds nothing, so it takes no payload:

let id: int64 | str | none = "abc"

match id {
    int64(n) if n < 0 -> print("negative")
    int64(n) -> print_int(n)
    str -> print("text")
    none -> print("nothing")
}

if id is str(s) {
    print(s)
}

On a value whose type is exactly T, T(name) always matches and binds the value, so it covers every case on its own: int64(n) on an int64, Shape(s) on a Shape, or T(x) in a generic function whatever T turns out to be. On a union, T has to be a member otherwise, or a union or optional whose members all are: on an int64 | str | bool, Id(i) with type Id = int64 | str matches an int64 or a str and binds it as an Id, and with type MaybeInt = int64?, MaybeInt(n) on an int64 | str | none matches an int64 or none. That is also what T(t) does in a generic function when T is a union or an optional. When two arms cover the same member, the first one wins. A member's type is written as it is declared, pa.Pt(p) for a type of another module; a member with no name of its own, such as [str], needs a type alias to be matched by type.

On a T or Error, a type pattern tests the value of an Ok, and Error(e) is Err(e) (see Fallible types).

On an interface, T is a struct or enum that implements it, and the pattern is a downcast, so a match still needs an else:

func describe(anon s: Shape) -> str {
    match s {
        Circle(c) if c.r > 10 -> return "big circle"
        Circle(c) -> return f"circle {c.r}"
        Square -> return "a square"
        else -> return "something else"
    }
}

An optional takes these patterns directly, like any pattern that can't match none (see Optional), whether it holds the type itself, a union or an interface. int64(n) on an int64? is Some(n), and on an int64 | str | none it is Some(int64(n)), which is also valid:

let maybe: int64 | str | none = "here"

match maybe {
    int64(n) -> print_int(n)
    str(s) -> print(s)
    none -> print("nothing")
}

The same holds inside another pattern. In a payload position a name that names a type is that type's pattern, not a binding: on a field of type int64 | str | none, .Full(str) tests and .Full(str(s)) binds, next to .Full(none). That's why a local can't take a type's name (see Bindings and mutability). An error for a missing arm spells it the same way, as doesn't cover `str`. A let-else takes it too: let str(s) = id else { return }.

items.title: is test
items.text:
A lightweight check without destructuring:

if x is none {
    print("empty")
}
if x is not none {
    print("has value")
}

items.title: Narrowing
items.text:
After an if tests a name, the name has the type the test proves inside the block that runs, with no new name to bind:

func describe(anon shape: Shape, anon id: int64 | str | none) -> none {
    if shape is Circle {
        print_int(shape.r)          // a Circle here
    }
    if id is not none {
        print(f"{id is str}")       // an int64 | str here
    }
    if id is none {
        print("no id")
    } else if id is int64 {
        print_int(id + 1)           // an int64 here
    }
}

x is T, x is Some, x is Ok, x is Err and x is not none narrow the block, and the later operands of an and chain, as in if x is not none and x > 3. x is none and x is not T narrow the else block. Narrowing is a binding of the same name, as x is T(x) would make, so it applies only when:

  • x is a plain name, such as a local or a parameter, not a field or a call;
  • the type is written by its own name, not through a module: m.T doesn't narrow, so bind it, as in if e is errs.NotFound(nf);
  • the block doesn't assign to x, which then keeps its declared type there.

After the block, x has its declared type again. A for condition doesn't narrow.

An early exit narrows the rest of its block too. After an if with no else whose block ends in return, throw, break, continue or panic(...), the statements that follow in the same block run only when the test failed:

func total(anon xs: [int64?], limit: int64 or Error) -> int64 {
    if limit is Err(e) {
        print(e.to_str())
        return 0
    }
    mut sum = 0                     // limit is an int64 from here on
    for x in xs {
        if x is none {
            continue
        }
        sum += x                    // x is an int64 from here on
    }
    if sum > limit {
        return limit
    }
    return sum
}

x is none, x is Err and x is not T narrow this way, under the rules above, with the rest of the block in place of the else block. The block has to end in the exit: a return, throw, break or continue, or a call that never returns, which is panic(...) or a function or method that can't finish by the rules in return (a -> none function with no return that ends in such a call, or in a for true loop without a break):

func fail(anon msg: str) -> none {
    panic(f"config: {msg}")
}

func port(anon raw: str?) -> int64 {
    if raw is none {
        fail("no port")
    }
    return raw.parse_int()? or 80   // raw is a str from here on
}

A call through a function value or an interface value is taken to return, so it doesn't narrow, and neither does a block that ends in an if whose branches all return. When the call can return, the rest of the block sees the name as it was.

items.title: Nested patterns
items.text:
A payload position can hold a pattern instead of a name. The arm matches only when every nested pattern does, and a failed test moves on to the next arm:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

match shape {
    .Rect(w, 0)     -> print(f"flat {w}")   // h must be 0, w is bound
    .Rect(_, _)     -> print("rect")
    .Circle(radius) -> print_int(radius)
}

let best: Shape? = find_best()
match best {
    Some(.Circle(r))  -> print_int(r)
    Some(.Rect(w, h)) -> print_int(w * h)
    none              -> print("nothing")
}

Patterns nest to any depth, and each kind above can appear inside another: literals, none, Some(...), Ok(...), Err(...), enum variants, and a type pattern such as .Wrap(Sq(s)) or .Wrap(Sq). In a payload position a bare name binds, unless it names a type. A nested literal needs a field of its own type.

Tests run left to right and from the outside in, and each nested pattern sees the field's type, so .Pair(Some(0), "x") needs an optional int64 and a str.

Nested patterns work wherever a pattern can bind: in a match, in an if or for condition (if best is Some(.Circle(r)) { ... }), and in a let-else (let .Some(.Circle(r)) = best else { return }). Elsewhere is is only a test, and a nested pattern is an error: use a match, or an if of its own.

items.title: Guards
items.text:
An arm's pattern can be followed by if and a condition. The arm runs only when the pattern matches and the condition is true; otherwise the next arm is tried. The pattern's bindings are in scope in the guard:

match shape {
    .Circle(r) if r > 100 -> print("big circle")
    .Circle(r)            -> print_int(r)
    .Rect(w, h) if w == h -> print("square")
    .Rect(_, _)           -> print("rect")
}

The guard must be a bool. It runs at most once for each arm, after that arm's pattern has matched, and can call functions. On an arm with alternatives it applies to each of them: .Plus | .Minus if ready -> .... Guards work in match statements and match expressions, but not on else, which has no pattern to guard. A guard can't bind names itself; put the pattern in the arm instead: Some(.Circle(r)) -> ... rather than Some(s) if s is .Circle(r) -> ....

items.title: Alternatives (|)
items.text:
Patterns joined with | share an arm, in a match statement or expression:

match token {
    .Plus | .Minus -> print("additive")
    .Star | .Slash -> print("multiplicative")
    else print("other")
}
match n {
    1 | 2 | 3 -> print("small")
    else print("big")
}

The arm counts as one arm for each alternative when the compiler checks that a match is exhaustive. Alternatives can't bind names, because each would have to bind the same ones; _ and nested literals are fine, as in .Circle(_) | .Dot and .Rect(0, _) | .Rect(_, 0). Give an arm that binds a line of its own.

items.title: Match as expression
items.text:
A match produces a value when every arm has a value, in the simplest case a single expression:

let label: str = match direction {
    .North -> "north"
    .South -> "south"
    .East  -> "east"
    .West  -> "west"
}

Payload, Some(x), and Ok(v) / Err(e) bindings are in scope in the arm's expression, just as in the statement form. They may hide a local of the same name, which is back after the arm (see Blocks and bindings):

let area: int64 = match shape {
    Shape.Circle(r)  -> 3 * r * r
    Shape.Rect(w, h) -> w * h
}

Without an annotation, the match takes the type of its first arm that isn't none, and each arm's bindings have that arm's payload types:

let name = match w {
    .S(value) -> value          // value: str
    .I(value) -> f"#{value}"    // value: int64
}
print(name + "!")               // name: str

A none arm, or an arm of type T? next to arms of type T, makes the match a T?, and the plain arms are wrapped: let found = match k { 1 -> "one" else -> none } is a str?. Every other arm must have the match's type, so 1 -> "a" next to else -> 2 is an error. With an annotation each arm is converted to the annotated type, which is how arms of different structs become one interface value: let s: Shape = match k { 1 -> Sq(s: 2) else -> Circle(r: 1) }.

When the match's value is used, every arm needs a value: an arm that calls a function returning none is an error, unless the call never returns, like panic(...) or a helper that ends in one, an imported module's function (log.die(...)) included (see Return values). In a -> none or -> none or Error function, return match k { 1 -> a() else -> b() } doesn't use the value, so its arms may return none. Without an annotation, a match whose arms are all none is an error too, as let x = none is, since its type can't be inferred.

items.title: Arms with several statements
items.text:
An arm of a match expression may be a block. Its last statement must be an expression, and that expression is the arm's value; the statements before it run first, and what they bind is gone after the arm:

let size: int64 = match shape {
    Shape.Circle(r) -> {
        let d = 2 * r
        d * 3
    }
    Shape.Rect(w, h) -> w * h
}

The block is an ordinary block, so it may return, throw or try (they leave the function, not just the arm), and an arm without braces is still one expression. else { ... } takes a block too. A block that is empty, or whose last statement is not an expression (let, if, an assignment), is an error: the arm would have no value. A match statement needs none of this, since its arms are blocks already.

items.title: if X is .Variant(bindings) { ... }
items.text:
When you want a one-arm match with bindings in scope for the body, the if/is sugar is shorter than a full match:

if module.decls[i] is .Func(decl_id) {
    // decl_id is in scope here
}

An optional else { ... } runs when the pattern doesn't match, and else if chains on as it does after any if; that if can bind names of its own: if r is Ok(v) { … } else if r is Err(e) and e.code > 0 { … }. Pattern bindings stay scoped to the matching arm — they aren't in scope in the else block. There and after the if, a name the pattern binds means what it meant before the if, such as an outer local it hid in the arm: in if o is Some(o) { … } else { … } the else block's o is the optional. As in a match arm, the pattern can name the enum, if s is Shape.Rect(w, h), or an imported one, if s is geo.Shape.Rect(w, h).

On a T? value, .Some(v) and .None are the same patterns as Some(v) and none, here, in a match and with a bare is. On a T or Error value, .Ok(v) and .Err(e) are the same as Ok(v) and Err(e). Naming the enum works too, as in Result.Ok(v). A generic enum is named without type arguments, and the bindings take the value's payload types: on a Maybe[int64], Maybe.Just(n) binds an int64.

Any other variant pattern needs an enum value, or an optional of one, where it tests the value inside: on a Color?, .Red matches a .Red and not none. Likewise .Some and .None need an optional, and .Ok and .Err a T or Error.

A bare is also tests an enum value's variant without binding its payload: if c is .Red and ready { ... }, s is .Circle(_).

A pattern with bindings can also be one of the operands an if condition joins with and. Its names are in scope in the operands after it and in the body, as if each is were its own if nested inside the one before:

if decl is .Import(_path, alias, _items) and not alias.starts_with("#") {
    aliases += [alias]
}
if a is .Some(x) and b is .Some(y) and x == y {
    print_int(x)
} else {
    print("no match")
}

The else block runs when any operand fails, and sees none of the bindings. A for condition can bind the same way (see for). Elsewhere a pattern can't bind: not under or or not, not with is not inside an and chain, not in a let value. There the is is only a test, and .Circle(r) is an error.

if v is .Some(x) {
    print_int(x)
} else {
    print("missing")
}

items.title: let .Pattern(bindings) = expr else { ... }
items.text:
Destructure with an early-exit on the non-matching case. The else block must exit the enclosing scope (return / throw / panic, or break / continue in a loop) so the bindings are guaranteed-in-scope below. A block that can reach its end is an error, decided by the same rules as the end of a function (see Return values): it may end in an if/else or a match whose every branch exits, in a for true loop it can't break out of, or in a call that never returns, as for match arms above:

let .Some(v) = m.get(key) else { return -1 }
// v is in scope here

The bindings start after the else block, so inside it a name the pattern binds still has the binding it had before the let-else, if any.

The pattern is a variant with its payload, as in .Some(v), Some(v), Ok(v) or Shape.Circle(r), or a type pattern such as str(s) (see Type patterns). On a T? value (like m.get(key) above), .Some(v) binds the unwrapped payload and .None matches none. On a T or Error value, .Ok(v) binds the value and .Err(e) the error. On an enum value, the variant is looked up in that value's enum, even when another enum declares a variant of the same name:

let .Ok(text) = read_text(path) else { return 1 }
print(f"{text}!")    // text is a str

items.title: Exhaustiveness
items.text:
A match on an enum (or on T?, a union or bool) must cover every variant. The compiler reports an error if any variant is missing and no wildcard arm is present. An arm naming a variant the enum doesn't declare is reported instead, since it's usually a misspelling of the missing one, and its bindings don't cause further errors in the arm.

type Color = enum {
    Red
    Green
    Blue
}

let c: Color = .Red
// error: match on Color doesn't cover variant Blue
match c {
    .Red -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
}

An arm with a guard doesn't cover anything, since its condition can be false: some other arm has to handle that variant too.

Nested patterns are checked all the way down. These arms cover every Shape?, so no else is needed:

match best {
    Some(.Circle(_))  -> print("circle")
    Some(.Rect(_, _)) -> print("rect")
    none              -> print("nothing")
}
