Drop the .Rect arm and the error names what is left: match onShape?doesn't coverSome(.Rect(_, _))`. A nested literal never completes a field of typeint64orstr, so.Rect(w, 0)` needs another arm for the same variant.

Add the missing arm or an else catch-all:

match c {
    .Red -> print("red")
    .Green -> print("green")
    else -> print("other")
}

The single-arm sugar (if X is .V(b) { ... } and let .V(b) = X else { ... }) is not subject to exhaustiveness — they're explicitly one-variant checks.

A match on int64 or str must include an else arm — the compiler reports an error otherwise. (int64 and str have too many possible values to enumerate; the else makes the fall-through explicit.)

items.title: Hello, world
items.text:
Create hello.kod:

func main() -> int64 {
    print("Hello, world!")
    return 0
}

Build and run:

$ uv run kod build hello.kod
$ ./build/apps/hello/hello
Hello, world!

uv run kod run hello.kod does both in one step.

items.title: A real program
items.text:
func greet(anon name: str) -> none {
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let names: [str] = ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]
    for name in names {
        greet(name)
    }
    return 0
}

items.title: Variables
items.text:
Bindings are declared with let and are immutable — the name can't be reassigned. A type annotation is usually required:

let x: int64 = 42
let s: str = "hello"
let flag: bool = true

For a binding you intend to reassign, use mut:

mut count: int64 = 0
count = count + 1   // ok

let limit: int64 = 10
limit = 20          // error: cannot reassign immutable binding `limit`

items.title: A test file
items.text:
// arithmetic_test.kod
test "addition" {
    assert 2 + 2 == 4
}

test "subtraction" {
    assert 10 - 3 == 7
}

$ uv run kod test arithmetic_test.kod
ok   addition
ok   subtraction

2/2 passed
