items.title: Self-hosting
items.text: Kod's compiler is written in Kod and compiles itself. A checked-in binary of it, the snapshot, is what builds it from source.

items.title: Status
items.text:
The self-hosted compiler sh_kodc exists and is the production path. make stage1 builds it, and every kod build / kod run / kod test invocation uses it for codegen when available.

Sources in Kod:

File Role stdlib/kod/lexing.kod Tokenizer stdlib/kod/parsing.kod Parser (AST built into a pool of int64 ids) stdlib/kod/ast.kod AST node types stdlib/kod/regalloc.kod Register allocation over the emitted instructions stdlib/kod/codegen.kod ARM64 assembly emitter stdlib/kod/build.kod Import resolution and whole-program registration kodc.kod sh_kodc entry point: compile a module, emit the _main shim tools/kod.kod The native kod driver: build / run / test / check

sh_kodc reads a .kod file and emits ARM64 assembly to stdout, plus a few internal subcommands (_compile, _emit-runtime-main, _emit-test-runtime-main).

items.title: Build chain
items.text:
bootstrap/sh_kodc   checked-in sh_kodc snapshot
build/stage0/       C runtime objects, the always-linked stdlib modules, and the
                    compiler library shared by sh_kodc and the kod driver
build/stage1/       sh_kodc + its .s/.o, plus runtime_main.{s,o}
build/apps/kod/     the native kod driver
build/apps/<stem>/  the final executable; its objects are in <stem>.obj/, a tree that
                    mirrors the source tree (see Modules, "Symbol and object names")
link.cfg            how everything is linked, read by the Makefile and by kod

Driven by the Makefile:

  1. stage0: the checked-in snapshot bootstrap/sh_kodc compiles the always-linked stdlib modules and the compiler library to assembly; as assembles them and clang builds arena.c, rc.c and runtime.c.
  2. stage1: the snapshot compiles kodc.kod and writes the _main shim; clang links everything into build/stage1/sh_kodc. So sh_kodc is the current compiler sources, compiled by the snapshot.
  3. apps: kod build foo.kod compiles each of the program's modules with build/stage1/sh_kodc to build/apps/foo/foo.obj/<path>.o and links them against build/stage0/.

Two consequences: a codegen change reaches user programs right away, but the stage0 stdlib modules keep the snapshot's codegen until make bootstrap-snapshot refreshes it. And the compiler sources themselves may only use features the snapshot can compile.

There is no other way in: without the snapshot, make stops and says how to restore it. See Refreshing the snapshot and Recovering from a bad snapshot.

items.title: The link configuration
items.text:
link.cfg at the repository root describes the link once. The Makefile includes it and tools/kod.kod reads it, so both link the same way. One NAME := word word ... per line, and nothing else:

  • A name is capital letters, digits and _, starting with a letter, and is set once per file.
  • Words are separated by one space. A word is letters, digits and the characters _ . / , = + @ -; there is no quoting, no $(...), no continuation line, no tab, no trailing space.
  • A line that starts with # is a comment, and an empty line is skipped. A # anywhere else in a line is an error, and so is a comment that ends in \.

kod rejects a line that does not fit, naming the file and line; for a line that fits, Make and kod read the same words. link.local.cfg (untracked) is read after link.cfg and overrides single names on one machine; a new git worktree needs its own copy. It overrides and does not add: a name there that link.cfg does not set (a typo, or a name of Make's own such as STAGE0 or SHELL) is an error in both. Neither accepts a LINK, RUNTIME_C or STAGE0_KOD that ends up empty.

Name Meaning LINK command that links an executable: clang -target arm64-apple-darwin -Wl,-dead_strip. clang finds the SDK and the macOS version. CC, CFLAGS compile a C file: clang, -target arm64-apple-darwin -I stdlib -O2. The target is pinned as in LINK (and as), so a clang that follows the architecture of the shell it runs in (one under Rosetta) does not produce x86_64 objects that the arm64 link rejects. RUNTIME_C C files linked into every program; built to build/stage0/<name>.o STAGE0_KOD Kod modules linked into every program, in link order; prebuilt by the snapshot compiler to build/stage0/_<basename>.o, so their basenames must be unique

A program links, in order: LINK, -o <exe>, the RUNTIME_C objects, the STAGE0_KOD objects, the program's module objects, the objects of the C files its modules name, its _main shim, and last the arguments its modules give with kod:link (see Modules). A module that declares such lines cannot be in STAGE0_KOD, nor be one of the compiler's own modules: the Makefile does not read them. kod says so for STAGE0_KOD, and a test checks the others. Adding an always-linked module is one more word in STAGE0_KOD; the Makefile derives its rule. make rebuilds the C runtime objects and relinks sh_kodc and kod when link.cfg or link.local.cfg changes (the objects also when a header in stdlib/ does, such as kod_rt.h), and also when the configuration in force is not the one they were built with (it keeps that in build/.link-config), so removing link.local.cfg, or a name from it, rebuilds too. A program gets the deployment target of the machine that builds it, as clang chooses it (MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET in the environment overrides that).

Requirements: clang and as (Xcode Command Line Tools). kod is run from the repository root; from another directory uv run kod says that build/apps/kod/kod is not found, and that tool, called by its path, says link.cfg not found. Calling build/apps/kod/kod directly does not rebuild build/stage0/, so after a change to runtime.c or link.cfg run make kod (or uv run kod, which does); when the configuration names an always-linked object that is not there yet, kod says build/stage0/_name.o not found; run make.

items.title: Refreshing the snapshot
items.text:
make bootstrap-snapshot

Runs make selfhost-check, checks that the stage2 and stage3 binaries are byte-identical, and only then copies the stage2 sh_kodc over bootstrap/sh_kodc. It takes seconds. Commit the new binary on its own.

A feature takes two steps to reach the compiler's own sources: commit the feature, refresh the snapshot, and only then use it there. The compiler sources may use only what the snapshot can compile.

Don't rewrite the history of bootstrap/sh_kodc: each old version can build the sources of its time, which makes them the way back.

The snapshot is arm64-darwin only. Bringing the compiler to another platform means adding the target and cross-compiling from a Mac.

items.title: Recovering from a bad snapshot
items.text:
The fixed-point check shows that a compiler reproduces itself, not that it is right: a snapshot with a bug that reproduces itself passes. If bootstrap/sh_kodc is lost or bad:

  1. Restore a good version from git, the newest one before the problem: git log -- bootstrap/sh_kodc, then git checkout <rev> -- bootstrap/sh_kodc. If it can't compile the current sources, check out the sources of that commit as well and work forward one snapshot at a time.
  2. As a last resort, the tag python-bootstrap is the last commit with the Python interpreter, which builds the compiler with no binary at all: check it out and run make bootstrap-snapshot (about 11 minutes). From that compiler, work forward through later commits the same way.

items.title: What's still Python
items.text:
• kod/__main__.py: uv run kod build|run|test|check, run from the repository root, refreshes the toolchain with make and hands off to build/apps/kod/kod. If make fails, it prints make's errors and kod: failed to rebuild the toolchain and stops with make's status; from any other directory, or when make is not installed and the tool is not built, it says that the tool is missing.
  • tests/ and tools/asm_diff.py: the test harness and the assembly comparison.

Tests call build/apps/kod/kod and build/stage1/sh_kodc directly. uv tool install . is not supported: the wheel contains no stdlib.

items.title: Codegen design
items.text:
codegen.kod is a single-pass emitter built around a few key data structures:

  • Expression / statement / type-expr pools on the parser: AST nodes are stored in flat arrays and referenced by int64 ids.
  • Struct / enum / interface tables on the codegen: registration happens before compilation; field/method lookups index these tables. Each module also keeps a table of the type names it declares, so a type name resolves in the module that wrote it: through that module's own table, the tables of the modules its import lists name, then the builtins', and m.T through the table of the module imported as m.
  • Register pool: x8–x15 used as expression temporaries; saved/restored across calls via stack spills as needed. Code nested too deeply for the pool saves every live register to frame slots and compiles with all of them free, so nesting has no fixed limit.
  • Generic monomorphisation: each unique Map[str, int64] instantiation gets its own struct entry; methods compile once per instantiation.
  • Interface dispatch: {data_ptr, vtable_ptr} cells on the heap, one vtable per (struct, interface) pair; primitives box implicitly.

items.title: Verifying self-hosting
items.text:
make selfhost-check

Fixed-point check. build/stage1/sh_kodc compiles the compiler into build/selfhost/stage2/, that compiler compiles it again into build/selfhost/stage3/, and the two sets of assembly must be byte-identical. A miscompile in the compiler that changes its own behavior shows up as a difference. Takes a few seconds; pytest runs it.

It then compiles every .kod file in the repo (the make asm-diff corpus) with both build/stage1/sh_kodc and the stage2 compiler, and fails if any file's assembly, diagnostics or exit status differ, writing both outputs under build/selfhost/corpus-diff/. Stage1 is the current sources compiled by the snapshot and stage2 the same sources compiled by themselves, so a difference means the snapshot miscompiles some of the new compiler code, typically a construct it handles differently than the current compiler does. Compiler sources must then avoid that construct until the snapshot is refreshed.

items.title: Checking that a compiler refactor changes nothing
items.text:
make asm-diff            # compare against HEAD
make asm-diff BASE=main  # or any other revision

Builds sh_kodc at BASE (cached under build/asm-diff/), compiles every .kod file in the repo with both that compiler and the working tree's, and reports each file whose assembly, diagnostics or exit status differ. A pure refactor should report no differences. Both compilers read the working tree's stdlib/, so the comparison isolates changes to the compiler itself.

items.title: Strings
items.text: Strings in Kod are UTF-8 byte sequences. The type is str.

items.title: Literals
items.text:
let s: str = "hello, world"

Supported escape sequences:

Escape Meaning \n newline \t tab \r carriage return \0 NUL byte \\ backslash \" double quote \' single quote \xHH the byte HH, two hex digits (00 to FF) \u{H...} a Unicode character, 1 to 6 hex digits, written as UTF-8

\x gives a single byte, so "\xC3\xA9" and "\u{e9}" are both é (two bytes), while "\xE9" is one byte that isn't valid UTF-8 by itself. A string may hold any bytes. A \u{...} must be a Unicode scalar value: at most 10FFFF, and not a surrogate (D800 to DFFF).

A malformed \x or \u is an error: a \x without two hex digits, a \u without braces, an empty or unterminated \u{}, more than six digits, or a value that isn't a scalar value. For any other escape the backslash and the character after it are both dropped, so "\q" is "". Non-ASCII UTF-8 can also be written directly in the source. Character literals ('a') take the simple escapes only.

Byte literals (b"...") and f-strings take the same escapes. In an f-string, the braces of \u{...} are part of the escape, not an interpolation: f"\u{e9}{n}" is é followed by the value of n.

items.title: F-strings
items.text:
Interpolate expressions into strings with f"...":

let name: str = "world"
print(f"hello, {name}!")          // hello, world!

let n: int64 = 42
print(f"the answer is {n}")       // the answer is 42

Anything inside { } is a Kod expression, string literals and nested f-strings included (f"[{f"<{n}>"}]", f"{"}" + s}"). Non-str values are auto-converted via their to_str method:

print(f"{a} + {b} = {a + b}")
print(f"flag={true}")             // flag=true
print(f"items: {items.len()}")    // any type with to_str works

Interpolations are evaluated left to right, as are the operands of an operator or a comparison chain, the parts of xs[i] and xs[lo..hi], and the receiver, index and value of a store such as xs[i] = v, so in f"{bump(:c)} then {c.n}" the second part sees what bump did.

What can be interpolated:

  • str, and bytes as-is
  • int64 and bool
  • a struct that declares func to_str(self) -> str
  • a value of an interface that declares the same to_str, such as Stringable or Error; the call goes to the concrete type's to_str
  • an enum, by its func to_str(self) -> str if it declares one, and otherwise as the name of its variant: f"{c}" is Red, and an Op.Lit(n: 4) is Lit, without its payload. A T or Error isn't one of these: test it first

print(x) takes the same values as {x} does.

Anything else is a compile error for now: an optional (T?), an array, a function value, and a struct or interface without a func to_str(self) -> str, including one whose to_str takes arguments or returns something else. Unwrap an optional first, e.g. f"{n? or 0}".

The braces hold one expression, which may be followed by a format spec.

items.title: Format specs
items.text:
After a :, a format spec says how wide the text is and how a number is written, as in Python:

let n = 42
let x = 3.14159
let name = "kod"
print(f"[{n:5}] [{n:<5}] [{n:^5}] [{n:05}] [{n:+}]")  // [   42] [42   ] [ 42  ] [00042] [+42]
print(f"{x:.2} {x:8.3} {x:e} {0.25:.1%}")            // 3.14    3.142 3.141590e+00 25.0%
print(f"{255:x} {255:#X} {5:08b} {1234567:,}")        // ff 0XFF 00000101 1,234,567
print(f"[{name:>6}] [{name:*^7}] [{"truncated":.5}]")  // [   kod] [**kod**] [trunc]

The parts, in this order, each optional:

Part Meaning fill and align < left, > right, ^ centred, after an optional fill character (a space if none). Numbers align right and everything else left unless told otherwise. sign + writes a + before a positive number, and a space writes a space there; a negative number always has its -. # Puts 0x, 0X, 0o or 0b before a number written in that base. 0 Pads a number with zeros after its sign and base prefix, to the width. width The least number of characters (code points); a longer value isn't cut. , or _ Groups the digits of a decimal number in threes, or with _ those of a hex, octal or binary number in fours. .precision For a float, the digits after the point; for a string, the most characters to keep. type For an int64: d decimal (the default), x and X hex, o octal, b binary. For a float64: f fixed point (six digits after the point unless a precision says), e exponent form (3.141590e+00), % the value times 100 with a %. For a string: s.

A float without a type or precision is written as {x} writes it, then padded; with a precision and no type, it has that many digits after the point. Digits are rounded correctly from the float's exact value, ties to even. A bool, an enum or a struct is formatted as the text {x} gives it, so only the fill, align, width and precision apply.

A spec that doesn't fit the value is a compile error: {n:.2} on an int64, {x:x} on a float64, {name:05} on a str. The spec is written out, so {n:{w}} with a width taken from a variable is an error too.

The same specs are also methods: n.format("05"), x.format(".2") and s.format(">10") give what f"{n:05}" and the others do.

items.title: Concatenation
items.text:
Use + to concatenate strings, or += to append in place:

let greeting: str = "hello" + ", " + name + "!"

mut buf: str = "lines:\n"
buf += "  one\n"
buf += "  two\n"

+= works on struct fields too: obj.message += " (cont.)".

Both operands of + must be str; nothing else is converted, so "n = " + 5 is an error. Convert with str(...) or use an f-string: "n = " + str(n) or f"n = {n}". bytes concatenate only with bytes.

items.title: Multi-line strings
items.text:
Triple-quoted strings span multiple lines:

let preamble: str = """
    .text
    .globl _main
    _main:
    """

The closing """ must sit on its own line. Its indent anchors the dedent — every content line has at least that many leading spaces (or tabs) stripped. The newline immediately after the opening """ is not part of the value; the newline before the closing """ is. So the example above produces:

.text
.globl _main
_main:

(four-space indent gone; trailing newline kept).

Combine with f for interpolation:

let asm: str = f"""
    bl ${mangled}$main
    ret
    """

Escape sequences work the same as in regular strings. Each content line must be indented at least as far as the closing """; a content line with less indent is a lex error.

items.title: Length
items.text: let n: int64 = len(s)

items.title: Character access
items.text:
Index into a string to get the ASCII value of a character (as int64):

let c: int64 = s[0]   // 'h' → 104

Negative indices count from the end:

let last: int64 = s[-1]

The index must be an int64, so s["a"] is an error.

Strings are immutable, so assigning to an element (s[0] = 'H') is an error. A str can't be iterated with for … in either; iterate over s.code_points() instead.

items.title: Slicing
items.text:
let sub: str = s[2..5]   // bytes at positions 2, 3, 4

Either endpoint may be omitted: s[..k] is s[0..k] and s[k..] is s[k..len(s)]. s[..] returns a copy.

Both endpoints clamp to [0, len(s)]: a negative bound becomes 0 and a bound past the end becomes len(s), so "hello"[3..40] is "lo". An end before the start yields "". Unlike indexing, slice bounds never wrap. Both bounds must be int64. bytes slices follow the same rules.

items.title: Comparison
items.text:
if s == "hello" {
    print("match")
}
if s != "bye" {
    print("not bye")
}

String equality compares contents, not identity. <, <=, > and >= order two strings byte by byte, a prefix before the longer string: "apple" < "apples" < "zebra". The same holds for two bytes values.

items.title: Searching and comparing
items.text:
All of these work on bytes. For text that must be split at code points, use code_points() or char_slice.

"GET /index".starts_with("GET")        // true
"a.kod".ends_with(".kod")              // true
"hello".contains("ell")                // true
"hello".find("l")                      // 2, an int64?
"hello".find("l", from: 3)             // 3
"hello".find("z")                      // none
"abc".strip_prefix("a")                // "bc", a str?
"abc".strip_suffix("x")                // none

find returns the byte offset of the first match at or after from (default 0; a from outside the string is clamped into it). The empty string is found at from. strip_prefix and strip_suffix return none when the string doesn't start or end that way. "" is a prefix and a suffix of every string.

items.title: Splitting, trimming and joining
items.text:
"a,b,,c".split(",")                    // ["a", "b", "", "c"]
"".split(",")                          // [""]
"abc".split("")                        // ["abc"]
"  hi\r\n".trim()                     // "hi"
"  hi ".trim_start()                   // "hi "
"  hi ".trim_end()                     // "  hi"
", ".join(["a", "b", "c"])             // "a, b, c"
"ab".repeat(3)                         // "ababab"
"a-b-c".replace("-", to: "+")        // "a+b+c"

split always returns at least one element and keeps empty pieces, so sep.join(s.split(sep)) == s for a non-empty sep. An empty separator doesn't split. trim removes space, tab, \n, \r from the ends. replace replaces every non-overlapping match from the left; an empty old replaces nothing. repeat with a count of 0 or less gives "".

items.title: Case and numbers
items.text:
"Content-Length".lower()               // "content-length"
"abc".upper()                          // "ABC"
"-42".parse_int()                      // -42, an int64?
"4x".parse_int()                       // none
"".parse_int()                         // none

lower and upper change only ASCII letters and leave other bytes alone. parse_int accepts an optional - or + followed by one or more decimal digits and nothing else (no spaces); it returns none for anything else and for a value outside the int64 range.

items.title: Building strings
items.text:
+= copies the whole string every time, so a loop that appends thousands of pieces does quadratic work. Use a StrBuilder for that:

import "strbuilder" { StrBuilder }

let out = StrBuilder()
out.append("HTTP/1.1 200 OK")
out.append("\r\n")
out.append_byte(10)
out.append_bytes(body)
print(out.to_str())
Method Meaning append(s: str) add a string append_bytes(b: bytes) add raw bytes append_byte(b: int64) add one byte; only the low 8 bits are used len() -> int64 bytes so far clear() drop the content, keep the capacity to_str() -> str a copy of the content; the builder stays usable to_bytes() -> bytes the same as bytes

The buffer doubles when it is full, so appending n bytes costs O(n) overall. to_str makes a StrBuilder usable in an f-string. Embedded NUL bytes are kept. A StrBuilder is a handle: copies of it (let b = a) share one buffer.

items.title: Conversion
items.text:
Primitives have a to_str method:

let s: str = 42.to_str()           // "42"
let t: str = true.to_str()         // "true"
let u: str = "hi".to_str()         // identity

Structs can opt in by declaring func to_str(self) -> str. F-string interpolation calls to_str automatically. str(x) converts the same values an f-string interpolates, and rejects the same ones.

See Built-ins for the full list of string-related functions.

items.title: Structs
items.text: Structs are named product types — a fixed set of named fields.

items.title: Declaration
items.text:
type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64
}

Comments are allowed inside the body:

type Rect = struct {
    // top-left corner
    x: int64
    y: int64
    // dimensions
    width: int64
    height: int64
}

A field's type can name the struct itself:

type Node = struct {
    kids: [Node]
    parent: Node?
    name: str
}

items.title: Construction
items.text:
Pass fields by name using labeled arguments, in any order:

let p: Point = Point(x: 10, y: 20)
let q: Point = Point(y: 20, x: 10)   // the same point

The values are computed in the order they're written. Every value needs its label, so Point(10, 20) is an error at each value:

let p: Point = Point(10, 20)
// error: argument 1 of `Point` needs a field label (`x:`)
// error: argument 2 of `Point` needs a field label (`y:`)

Each unlabelled value is offered the next field, in declaration order, that no label names.

Every field must be supplied unless it has a default. Omitting a field with no default is a compile error — there's no implicit zero/null value:

let p: Point = Point(x: 10)   // error: struct `Point` requires field `y`

Each field value must have the field's type, with the same implicit conversions as a function argument: Point(x: "a", y: 1) is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), while 3 is fine for an int64? field and a struct for an interface field. A field can be given only once: Point(x: 1, x: 2, y: 3) is an error (field `x` is given twice).

items.title: Field defaults
items.text:
A field may declare a default with = expr. When a construction omits that field, the default expression is evaluated and stored:

type Counter = struct {
    label: str
    count: int64 = 0
    history: [int64] = []
}

let c: Counter = Counter(label: "hits")   // count = 0, history = []
let d: Counter = Counter(label: "x", count: 5)

The default is evaluated fresh at each construction (so a [] default yields a new empty array per instance, not a shared one). Defaults are ordinary expressions evaluated in the struct's defining module, and they can't see the local variables of the function doing the construction. A default must have its field's type, which is checked where it is declared, so count: int64 = "x" is an error even if no construction omits count. Anything else wrong in it, such as an unknown name or variant, is reported where a construction omits the field, and a generic struct's default is checked only at each construction that omits it.

This is what lets the built-in Map[K, V] be created with no arguments — all three of its fields default to []:

let m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()

items.title: Custom constructors
items.text:
A struct may declare its own constructor, a function named init inside the body with no self:

type Port = struct {
    number: int64

    func init(number: int64) -> Port or Error {
        if number < 1 or number > 65535 {
            throw BadPort(number: number)
        }
        return Port(number: number)
    }
}

let p = try Port(number: 8080)     // calls init

From then on Port(...) anywhere outside the struct's own functions calls init, with the usual rules for a function call: labels, defaults and skipped labels. The field constructor is not available there, so a label init doesn't declare is an error. init is the only way to make a Port, and whatever it checks holds for every Port at the moment it is made.

Inside the struct's own functions, init and the other methods, Port(...) is the field constructor as before. That is how init builds the value, and how methods such as op_add make a new one without going through the checks again. A method can't call init itself.

init must return the struct (-> Port) or a result of it (-> Port or Error), which makes try Port(...) and must Port(...) work as for any fallible call. It may not be a generic struct's: init on a Box[T] is an error for now. A struct without init is built from its fields as described above.

Public fields stay assignable, so p.number = 0 is still possible after a checked construction. To keep what init checks true for the value's whole life, make the field private.

items.title: Private fields
items.text:
A field whose name starts with _ is private: only the struct's own functions (init, its methods and its operator methods) can read or assign it, or name it in the field constructor.

type Duration = struct {
    _ns: int64

    func init(seconds: int64 = 0, ms: int64 = 0) -> Duration {
        return Duration(_ns: seconds * 1 000 000 000 + ms * 1 000 000)
    }

    func as_ms(self) -> int64 {
        return self._ns / 1 000 000
    }
}

let d = Duration(seconds: 5)
print_int(d.as_ms())    // 5000
d._ns                   // error: field `_ns` is private to `Duration`
d._ns = 0               // error: field `_ns` is private to `Duration`

Only Duration's own functions can set _ns, so whatever init checks about it holds for as long as the value lives. Callers depend only on the methods, so the representation can change without breaking them: Duration could store microseconds instead and no caller would notice.

Outside the struct, a private field can't be named in the field constructor either. A private field with a default is filled in from it; a private field without one means the struct can only be built through init or its own functions. Public and private fields mix freely.

Privacy covers the field, not what it points to. A method that returns a private array returns the array itself, which the caller can then change by indexing it; return a copy when that matters.

items.title: Private methods
items.text:
A method whose name starts with _ is private in the same way: only the struct's own functions can call it, as self._name(...) or on another value of the struct.

type Duration = struct {
    _ns: int64

    func _whole(self, unit: int64) -> int64 {
        return self._ns / unit
    }

    func as_ms(self) -> int64 {
        return self._whole(unit: 1 000 000)
    }
}

d.as_ms()               // fine
d._whole(unit: 1)       // error: method `_whole` is private to `Duration`

That keeps helpers that assume the struct's invariants, or that would break them, out of the struct's interface. A method of a primitive type such as str or int64 is private to the module that declares it.

An interface can't declare a private method: calling it through the interface would reach the struct's method from outside.

items.title: Field access
items.text:
print_int(p.x)
print_int(p.y)

items.title: Field mutation
items.text:
p.x = p.x + 1

Reading or assigning a field the struct doesn't declare is an error, with a did-you-mean hint when the name is close to a real field. So is .field on a value that isn't a struct, such as an interface or an optional; for a T?, use p?.x.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Define methods inside the struct body. The first parameter must be self:

type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64

    func distance_sq(self) -> int64 {
        return self.x * self.x + self.y * self.y
    }

    func translate(self, dx: int64, dy: int64) -> none {
        self.x = self.x + dx
        self.y = self.y + dy
    }
}

Call methods with dot notation:

let p: Point = Point(x: 3, y: 4)
print_int(p.distance_sq())   // 25
p.translate(dx: 1, dy: 0)
print_int(p.x)               // 4

Methods can also be invoked on non-Ident receivers — 0.to_str(), p.field.method(), f().bar(), etc.

A method's parameter and return types can name the struct itself or a type declared later in the module, so func scaled(self, by: int64) -> Point inside Point chains as p.scaled(by: 2).distance_sq().

items.title: Generic structs
items.text:
Type parameters in square brackets after the name; each unique instantiation is monomorphised:

type Pair[A, B] = struct {
    first: A
    second: B

    func swap(self) -> Pair[B, A] {
        return Pair[B, A](first: self.second, second: self.first)
    }
}

let p: Pair[str, int64] = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42)
let q = p.swap()    // Pair[int64, str]

Construction always spells the type arguments; a bare Pair(...) is an error.

A method of an instance is compiled for its type arguments when something uses it: a call, an operator or other syntax that calls it, or the instance becoming a value of an interface, which uses all of that interface's methods. So a Box[T] whose contains uses == can hold a struct that has no ==, as long as nothing calls contains on that Box. Only a method's signature is checked otherwise, so a mistake in the body of a method nothing uses isn't reported, as with a generic function nothing calls. An error in a body names the instance, as in `<` doesn't take `Color` operands; declare `op_lt` on `Color` to use it (in `Box[Color]`), and a line of the template is reported for one instance only.

A generic struct or enum may name itself, with any type arguments, in its fields, payloads and method signatures, as in kids: [Tree[T]] or the Pair[B, A] above. The instances have to end, though: one that keeps naming a bigger type, like next: W[[T]]? in W[T] or a called method of W[T] that makes a W[[T]], is an error once it is 64 instances deep (generic type `W` is 64 instances deep; each one names another with a new type). Methods that branch into new types are stopped earlier, when a module passes 4096 instances.

The built-in Map[K, V] is the canonical example.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
A struct gives the arithmetic and comparison operators a meaning by declaring methods with reserved names. The operator on the left operand's struct calls the method with the right operand as its one argument:

Operator Method Returns a + b op_add(self, other) any type a - b op_sub(self, other) any type a * b op_mul(self, other) any type a / b op_div(self, other) any type a % b op_mod(self, other) any type a == b, a != b op_eq(self, other) bool a < b, a > b, a <= b, a >= b op_lt(self, other) bool 
type Money = struct {
    cents: int64

    func op_add(self, other: Money) -> Money {
        return Money(cents: self.cents + other.cents)
    }

    func op_mul(self, times: int64) -> Money {
        return Money(cents: self.cents * times)
    }

    func op_eq(self, other: Money) -> bool {
        return self.cents == other.cents
    }

    func op_lt(self, other: Money) -> bool {
        return self.cents < other.cents
    }
}

let total = Money(cents: 250) + Money(cents: 100) * 3     // 550
if total > Money(cents: 500) { ... }

!= is not op_eq. The four orderings come from op_lt alone: a > b is b < a, a <= b is not (b < a) and a >= b is not (a < b). a += b and a -= b are a = a + b and a = a - b, and a < b < c chains as it does for numbers. The operators keep their usual precedence, and the operands are evaluated left to right whichever one the method belongs to.

A struct is the right operand when the left is an int64: 3 * price calls op_rmul on price with 3 as its argument. The reflected methods are op_radd, op_rsub, op_rmul, op_rdiv and op_rmod; each is tried only when the left operand isn't a struct, and there is no reflected comparison.

A method that implements an operator takes self and one more parameter, and the comparison methods return bool; otherwise it is an error where the operator is used. A struct that doesn't declare the method still can't use the operator, so a + b on a plain struct is the same error as before, and a == b still tells you to compare the fields. A prefix minus is 0 - x, so -price calls op_rsub with 0. not, and, or and is are never overloaded.

items.title: Memory layout (compiler)
items.text:
Struct fields are laid out sequentially, each taking 8 bytes, allocated on the heap:

[ offset 0  ] field_0 : 8 bytes
[ offset 8  ] field_1 : 8 bytes
...

Struct variables hold a pointer to the allocation.

items.title: Testing
items.text: Kod has built-in syntax for unit tests: test "description" { ... } blocks and an assert <expr> statement. kod test runs them.

items.title: A first test
items.text:
// arithmetic_test.kod
test "addition works" {
    assert 2 + 2 == 4
}

test "negative arithmetic" {
    assert -1 + 1 == 0
    assert -5 - 5 == -10
}

$ uv run kod test arithmetic_test.kod
ok   addition works
ok   negative arithmetic

2/2 passed

items.title: assert <expr>
items.text:
If the expression evaluates to false, the current test is marked failed and the source text of the expression is captured in the failure message — no need to type f"got {x}, want {y}":

test "this one will fail" {
    let n: int64 = 7
    assert n == 4
}

    foo_test.kod:3:5: assertion failed: n == 4
FAIL this one will fail

Multiple asserts per test continue running — they accumulate failure messages but don't short-circuit, so a single test surfaces every failing condition at once.

Outside a test block, assert panics with the same message (exit 1). Same syntax, intent matches the surrounding context — like Rust's always-on assert!.

items.title: fail(msg)
items.text:
For failures that aren't a boolean check, call the builtin fail:

test "map lookup hits" {
    let m: Map[str, int64] = Map[str, int64]()
    m.set("a", 1)
    match m.get("a") {
        Some(v) -> assert v == 1
        none -> fail("missing key after set")
    }
}

fail is a builtin — no import needed. It works from any function a test calls, not only inside the test block. Outside kod test there is no test to fail, so fail panics with its message, as assert does outside a test.

items.title: Discovery
items.text:
• kod test <file> builds the file and every transitively imported module that contains test blocks, then runs them all in one binary.
  • kod test <dir> walks the directory for *_test.kod and builds them all into one binary, with no temporary module. Each file keeps its own type names (see Modules), so two test files may both declare a helper type Pt, and two test files may share a file name (a/dup_test.kod and b/dup_test.kod).
  • kod test . walks the entire project.
  • The walk skips a file with a path component below the directory that starts with . (worktrees under .claude/, editor files, scratch files such as .kod_compile_test.kod) and a build directory directly below it. (The test suite's own finder skips the dot-directories and a top-level build/, but not dot-files.) Only files count: a directory named x_test.kod is walked, not run. A match that is not a readable file (a link to nothing) stops the run with kod test: cannot read <path>, since a test skipped without a word reads as one that passed. kod test <file> takes the file named, whatever its path.

The aggregate exit code is 0 if every test passed, non-zero otherwise.

items.title: Output
items.text:
kod test replaces itself with the test binary, so the output appears as the tests run, and the exit code is the binary's. The reporter flushes stdout around every ok/FAIL line and the file header, and before a failure's detail goes to stderr, so the lines stay in order when stdout and stderr are the same pipe or log. What a test prints with print is flushed with them, so it comes out before that test's result line. A panic (an index out of bounds, a failed must) flushes stdout before its message too.

When stdout is a terminal, ok is green, FAIL red, and the time each test took dim; the summary line is green when all passed and red when any failed. The same NO_COLOR and TERM=dumb turn this off as for errors.

items.title: Hermetic tests
items.text: A test needs nothing the repository does not have, and no network: a test of code that talks to a server starts a server of its own on the loopback interface. A test that needs the internet does not belong among the *_test.kod files that kod test <dir> and the test suite run. A module under test may declare C files and libraries (see Link inputs); kod test compiles and links them like kod build does, and a kod:require file that is missing stops the build, naming the line that asks for it.

items.title: Layout convention
items.text:
Test files live next to the code they test, Go-style:

stdlib/
  builtins.kod
  map_test.kod
  primitives/
    int64.kod
    int64_test.kod
    str.kod
    str_test.kod

The naming convention *_test.kod makes them auto-discoverable by kod test <dir> without showing up as importable modules.

items.title: How it works (briefly)
items.text:
• The parser turns test "..." { ... } into a Decl.Test carrying a synthesized FuncDecl.
  • The codegen emits each test as a regular function (<prefix>$__test_N) and, per module, a <prefix>$__run_tests dispatcher. <prefix> is described in Modules.
  • The runner is a Kod module, stdlib/testing.kod, which kod test links into every test program (and kod build into any program with a test block, since the block's code is linked even though nothing runs it). Its counters are module-level variables.
  • kod test builds a runtime _main that calls every test-bearing module's __run_tests in turn, then the runner's summary once at the end.
  • fail/assert set a per-test "failed" flag the dispatcher reads after each test returns; that flag drives the ok / FAIL line and the aggregate count.

items.title: Testing the compiler itself
items.text:
make test rebuilds the toolchain and runs pytest, which covers three kinds of check:

  • Example programs: every tests/**/*.kod. Trailing // expected output:, // expected errors:, // expected stderr:, // expected status: and // expected mode: comments say what should happen. Each one is compiled and run; mode: skip opts out, for a module other fixtures import.
  • Test blocks: every *_test.kod in the repo that contains test blocks runs through kod test <file>, one pytest case per file.
  • Self-hosting: the fixed-point check described in Self-hosting.

The tests run programs through the native tools, build/apps/kod/kod and build/stage1/sh_kodc; Python is only the test harness and the launcher.

make test runs most tests in parallel, one worker per core (with pytest-xdist). Tests that build the same program, into the same build/apps/<name>, share a group that one worker runs (tests/conftest.py decides the groups). The tests marked serial (those that rebuild or replace the kod driver, write into the project root, or run make on the real tree) run afterwards, one at a time. A plain uv run pytest runs everything one at a time, as before.

make gates is what to run before a commit: make test, then make test again with the runtime built with -DRC_POISON, which overwrites freed memory so a use after free shows up. It refuses to run when there is a link.local.cfg, since it writes its own for the poisoned pass, and removes it again however the pass ends.

items.title: Time
items.text:
stdlib/time.kod has two clocks, a Duration type, sleep, and a Time type for timestamps.

import "time"
import "time" { Duration }

let started = time.monotonic_ns()
time.sleep(Duration(ms: 250))
let took = Duration(ns: time.monotonic_ns() - started)
print(took.to_str())                       // 250.31ms

items.title: Clocks
items.text:
Function Returns monotonic_ns() nanoseconds from an unspecified origin that never go backwards; only differences mean anything. Use it to time things. unix_ns() nanoseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC by the wall clock. It can jump if the system clock is adjusted, so it is not for measuring elapsed time.

Both are plain int64, which holds about 292 years of nanoseconds.

items.title: Duration
items.text:
A Duration is a length of time, kept as nanoseconds in an int64 (ns). Make one by naming the units you want; they add up, and each defaults to 0:

Duration(seconds: 5)
Duration(ms: 250)
Duration(minutes: 1, seconds: 30)
Duration()                       // zero

The units are hours, minutes, seconds, ms, us and ns, and labels go in that order, largest first, as in Duration(seconds: 1, ms: 500). Duration is a struct with a custom constructor, so Duration(...) is the only way to build one from units, and the units are labels, not types: Duration(seconds: 90) and Duration(minutes: 1, seconds: 30) are equal.

items.title: Arithmetic and comparison
items.text:
Duration defines the operators:

let a = Duration(seconds: 2)
let b = Duration(ms: 500)
a + b                  // 2.5s
a - b                  // 1.5s
a * 3                  // 6s
3 * a                  // 6s
a / 4                  // 500ms
-a                     // -2s
a > b                  // true
a == Duration(ms: 2000)   // true

A duration times or divided by an int64 is a duration, and Duration has no Duration * Duration or Duration / Duration: use a.ns / b.ns for a ratio.

items.title: Methods
items.text:
Method Meaning as_ms() the whole milliseconds in it, truncated toward zero as_seconds() the whole seconds in it, truncated toward zero as_hours() the whole hours in it, truncated toward zero as_days() the whole 24-hour days in it, truncated toward zero ceil_ms() milliseconds, rounded up for a positive duration, so that a short timeout never becomes 0 (which most timeouts treat as none) to_str() a short reading, such as 1h2m3s, 1.5s, 250ms, 12.5us, 40ns or 0s

to_str writes hours and minutes only when the duration has them (a duration of an hour or more always shows minutes and seconds, as in 1h0m0s), seconds with a fraction when it has one, and below a second the largest unit that keeps the number at 1 or more. A negative duration starts with -.

items.title: Sleeping
items.text:
func sleep(anon d: Duration) -> none

waits at least d, to the resolution of the system clock, and a signal doesn't cut it short. A zero or negative duration returns at once.

items.title: Timestamps
items.text:
A Time is a moment: whole seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, negative before it, and nanos from 0 to 999999999 on top. It has no time zone of its own, and reads as UTC.

import "time"

let created = time.parse("2026-01-02T03:04:05+01:00")? or time.now()
print(created.to_str())                       // 2026-01-02T02:04:05Z
print(created.utc().year)                     // 2026
print((time.now() - created).as_days())       // how many days ago
Function Returns now() the wall clock's time parse(s) the Time of an RFC 3339 timestamp, or none if s isn't one parse_date(s) midnight UTC of a YYYY-MM-DD date, or none if s isn't one

parse takes what APIs send: 2026-01-02T03:04:05Z, with a fraction of a second as in 05.25Z, and an offset as in 05+01:00. A t and a z may be lowercase, as RFC 3339 allows. Digits past nanoseconds are dropped. It checks the calendar, so 2026-02-29 is none. A leap second, :60, is read as the first second after it, since a Time has no way to hold one.

Method Meaning t + d the Time a Duration later a - b the Duration from b to a, which wraps past about 292 years, as a Duration does a == b, a < b and the like whether they're the same moment, or which comes first utc() a Utc with year, month (1 to 12), day, hour, minute and second to_str() RFC 3339 in UTC, with a fraction only if there is one, as in 2026-01-02T02:04:05.25Z

items.title: Durations in other modules
items.text: The timeouts and deadlines of net/tcp, net/tls and the HTTP client are Durations: Client(deadline: Duration(seconds: 15)).

items.title: Types
items.text:
Kod is statically typed. Every parameter needs a type annotation; a let without one takes the type of its value.

Naming a type that doesn't exist is an error wherever a type is written: an annotation, a parameter or return type, a struct field, an enum payload, an alias target or a type argument. The error carries a did-you-mean hint when a known type name is close.

An unannotated let takes the type of its value. If the compiler can't work out that type, the binding is an error (cannot infer the type of `x`; add a type annotation), and so is any other use of such a value, like a match subject or an argument. A value whose type is unknown because of an earlier error, such as a call to an unknown function or method, a misspelled field, an unknown variant or an unknown type, doesn't produce further errors where it's used.

items.title: Bindings and mutability
items.text:
A let binding is immutable: once set, reassigning the name is a compile error. Use mut for a binding you need to reassign. += and -= count as reassignment, so they require mut too.

let max: int64 = 100
mut total: int64 = 0
total += max          // ok — total is mutable

max = 50              // error: cannot reassign immutable binding `max`

Mutability belongs to each binding. A let x in a block that hides an outer mut x (see Blocks and bindings) can't be reassigned inside that block, and after the block the outer x can be again. Likewise a mut x in a block leaves an outer let x immutable once the block ends. A for variable and the names a pattern binds, in a match arm, if … is or a let-else, can be reassigned without mut, whatever binding the name had in another block.

A local, whether a let, a parameter, a for variable or a pattern's binding, can't take the name of a type it can see: let str = 3 and for Circle in shapes are errors (`Circle` is the name of a type; give the local another name). In a pattern, a type's name is that type's pattern (see Type patterns).

Assigning to a name that was never declared is an error too (declare it with mut first), and so is assigning to anything other than a name, a field (p.x = 1) or an element (xs[0] = 1).

The value of an annotated let, of an assignment to a name and of an assignment to a field must have the declared type: let x: int64 = "s" is an error (expected `int64`, got `str`), and so is storing an int64 in a bool or an [int64] in a [str]. A T is accepted where a T? is declared and is checked as a T: with type Words = [str], let w: Words? = [] is fine and let w: Words? = [1] reports the element (expected `str`, got `int64`), while let x: int64? = "s" names the declared type (expected `int64?`, got `str`). none is accepted wherever an optional or none is declared, a struct or primitive other than bytes where an interface is, and [] as any array type. A T? isn't accepted where a T is declared; unwrap it first with x? or x? or default. An optional is passed on as it is, so a T? where a U? is declared needs T to be U: like an [Sq] isn't a [Shape], an Sq? or int64? isn't a Shape? even when Sq and int64 implement Shape; rewrap it instead, as in match sq { Some(v) -> v none -> none }. A function value must match a function type exactly, since a function is never adapted: a function taking a struct isn't a func(SomeInterface) -> ..., and one returning int64 isn't a func() -> int64?. Without an annotation, let x = none and let xs = [] are errors, since their type can't be inferred.

Function and method arguments, struct constructor fields and enum payloads are checked the same way (see Argument types), so m.set(5, 1) on a Map[str, int64] is an error. So are element stores (xs[i] = v, m[k] = v, see Indexing) and return values (see Return values).

Parameters are immutable too — mut makes one reassignable inside the body (mut self for a method receiver). This is callee-local: params are passed by value, so reassigning one never affects the caller, and the call site needs no annotation.

func bump(anon mut x: int64) -> int64 {
    x = x + 1     // ok — local to bump; the caller's value is unchanged
    return x
}

Struct fields stay mutable. And because structs and arrays are reference values (see Memory layout), mutating a struct's fields through a parameter or self (p.field = v) is still allowed regardless of whether the binding is mut — mut governs only reassigning the name.

items.title: Module-level constants
items.text:
A let at the top level of a module names a constant. It needs a type, and mut isn't allowed there:

let MAX_BLOCK: int64 = 65535
let SECONDS_PER_DAY: int64 = 24 * 60 * 60
let GREETING: str = "hello, " + "world"
let PRIMES: [int64] = [2, 3, 5, 7]
let DEFAULT_MODE: Mode = Mode.Fast

The value is built only from literals, operators, array literals, enum variants without a payload, and other constants. A call, a constructor, an f-string, a match or anything else is an error (this can't be part of a module-level constant), so a constant never has a side effect, and a constant that refers to itself, directly or through others, is an error (constant `A` refers to itself).

A constant is used by its name. Another module's is import "limits" { MAX_BLOCK } or limits.MAX_BLOCK, like a function's. A local variable or parameter of the same name hides it, as it does a function, and a constant and a function can't share a name in one module. A constant can't be assigned, and neither can its elements (`PRIMES` is a constant and can't be assigned; a module-level `mut` can be).

Each use of an array constant is an array of its own, so changing one changes nothing else: after let p = PRIMES and p[0] = 1, PRIMES[0] is still 2. A use that can't change the array, indexing it, len of it or a for over it, reads one copy that the program builds the first time and keeps, so a lookup table read in a loop allocates nothing. Indexing an array of arrays still makes a new array, since the element read could be changed. A string can't be changed, so a string constant is built once.

An int64 or bool constant whose value is literals and the operators +, -, *, &, |, ^, << and >> on them, like MAX_BLOCK and SECONDS_PER_DAY above, is worked out when the program is compiled and put in place at each use, and so is a float64 constant that is one literal: reading one costs what the literal would.

items.title: Module-level variables
items.text:
A mut at the top level of a module names a variable that every function of the program shares. Like a constant, it needs a type:

mut calls: int64 = 0
mut seen: Map[str, bool] = Map[str, bool]()
mut log_lines: [str] = []

func remember(anon name: str) -> bool {
    calls += 1
    if seen.contains(name) {
        return false
    }
    seen.set(name, true)
    log_lines += [name]
    return true
}

The value can be any expression, calls included. It is worked out once, the first time the program uses the variable (reads it or assigns it), so a variable nothing uses costs nothing, and the order in which modules are declared or imported doesn't matter. A value that needs its own variable to be worked out first, directly or through a function it calls, stops the program with panic: `calls` is used while its value is being worked out.

Another module reads a variable the way it reads a constant (import "stats" { calls } or stats.calls), but only the declaring module assigns it: `calls` can only be assigned in stats.kod. A value the variable holds can still be changed through its methods, fields and elements from anywhere (stats.seen.set(...)), as with any reference. A name that starts with _ keeps the variable private to its module. A local of the same name hides it, and a variable, constant or function can't share a name in one module. A constant can't use a variable, since a constant has no side effects (a module-level constant can't use the variable `calls`). A variable or constant that holds a function is called like one: mut on_error: func(str) -> none = log, then on_error("disk full").

Tests run in one program, one after another, so a test sees what the tests before it left in a module-level variable.

items.title: Primitive types
items.text: Type Description Example int64 64-bit signed integer 42, -7 float64 64-bit IEEE 754 float, see Floating point 1.5, 2e9 str UTF-8 string "hello" bool Boolean true, false none No value (unit type) —

items.title: Integer literals
items.text:
let n: int64 = 42
let m: int64 = -1

Base prefixes for non-decimal forms:

let hex: int64 = 0xff           // 255
let oct: int64 = 0o755          // 493
let bin: int64 = 0b1010         // 10

Decimal literals may use a space as a thousands separator. The grouping is strict — a head of 1-3 digits followed by space-prefixed groups of exactly 3 digits each:

let pop: int64 = 1 000 000      // ok
let bad: int64 = 1 23 456       // error — `23 456` isn't a group of 3, so it's another literal

A literal must fit in int64, in any base: 9223372036854775808 or 0x8000000000000000 is an error at the literal, not a value that wraps around. The one exception is the smallest int64, written as a prefix - and its digits, with or without a space between them: -9223372036854775808 or - 9223372036854775808. In x - 9223372036854775808 the - subtracts, and in -9223372036854775808.to_str() it negates the call, so in both the literal stands alone and is an error; the second suggests (-9223372036854775808).

Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, %. Compound assignment += and -= update a variable, field, or array element in place (n -= 3 is n = n - 3). An assignment binds looser than every operator, so ok = a and b assigns a and b. A prefix - negates the whole call, field access, index or ? after it, and binds tighter than any binary operator: -xs[0] is -(xs[0]), -p.get() is -(p.get()), and -a * b is (-a) * b. That includes an unwrap's default, so -x? or 3 is -(x? or 3) and gives -3 for a none. It also makes -n.to_str() the negation of a str, an error whose hint suggests (-n).to_str().

Integer / rounds toward zero and % takes the sign of its left operand, so -7 / 2 is -3 and -7 % 2 is -1, and (a / b) * b + a % b is always a. Dividing by zero, with / or %, panics: panic: integer division by zero, with a backtrace. The one quotient that doesn't fit, the smallest int64 divided by -1, wraps around to the smallest int64, and its remainder is 0.

>> shifts in zeros, so it treats an int64 as 64 bits rather than a signed number, and so do these methods, each a single instruction:

Method Gives n.leading_zeros() how many zero bits are above the highest one bit; 64 for 0 n.trailing_zeros() how many zero bits are below the lowest one bit; 64 for 0 n.count_ones() how many bits are one; 64 for -1 n.mul_high(m) the top 64 bits of the 128-bit product of n and m as unsigned numbers; n * m is the bottom 64 
print(1.leading_zeros())                // 63
print(40.trailing_zeros())              // 3
print(0xff.count_ones())                // 8
print((1 << 62).mul_high(8))            // 2

items.title: Boolean literals
items.text:
let flag: bool = true
let other: bool = false

Logical operators: and, or, not. Comparison: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=. Comparisons, and/or/not and is always produce a bool, so let ok = a < b is a bool binding and f"{a < b}" prints true or false.

not binds looser than comparisons and is, and tighter than and and or: not a == b is not (a == b), not x is .Red is not (x is .Red), and not a and b is (not a) and b. Its operand must be a bool; test an optional with x is none.

bool and int64 don't mix, and nothing else stands in for a bool. Both operands of and and or must be bool, and so must the condition of an if, a for loop and an assert: test a number with n != 0 and an optional with x is not none. Arithmetic, bitwise and ordering operators don't take bool operands, and ==/!= compare a bool only with another bool, so b == 1, true + 1 and if flags & 1 are errors. Comparisons bind tighter than &, | and ^, so a bit test is written (flags & 1) != 0.

Chained comparisons are supported Python-style: a < b < c is (a < b) and (b < c) with b evaluated once. The operands are evaluated left to right, and a chain stops at the first comparison that is false, so in a < b < f() f isn't called when a < b is false. Any comparison chain works — 0 <= i < len(xs) is the canonical bounds check.

items.title: Operators
items.text:
An operator never converts its operands; both must be of a type it takes, and of the same type:

Operator Operands Result + two int64, two float64, two str, two bytes or two arrays of one type the operands' type - * / two int64 or two float64 the operands' type % two int64 int64 & \| ^ << >> two int64 int64 < <= > >= two int64, two float64, two str or two bytes bool == != two int64, two float64, bool, str or bytes, two values of a payload-free enum, an enum value and a unit variant, an optional and none, or a union and a value that goes into it bool and or two bool bool

So "n = " + 5 is an error (cannot add `str` and `int64`); write "n = " + str(5) or f"n = {5}". s - t on two strings, xs * 2 on an array, -s on a string, s + b with b: bytes and red < blue on an enum are errors too. += and -= follow the rules of + and -. An index, as in xs[i], s[i] and xs[i] = v, and the bounds of a slice must be int64, so xs["a"] and xs[true] are errors, and so is an int64? index; unwrap it first.

== and != compare str and bytes by content and enums by variant (see Equality). Nothing else has an ==: comparing two structs, arrays, interface values or function values is an error, so compare a struct's fields, or an array's len(...) and elements, instead. Comparing values of two different types, like an int64 with a str or values of two different enums, is an error too.

items.title: none
items.text:
none is the unit value. Functions that return nothing are declared -> none:

func say_hi() -> none {
    print("hi")
}

items.title: Optional types
items.text:
Append ? to any type to make it optional:

let x: int64? = none
let y: int64? = 42

The ? goes after the whole type, so [str]? is an optional array and Box[int64]? an optional generic struct. names? or [] is the array, or an empty one when there is none.

Test with is and destructure with Some(binding):

if x is none {
    print("nothing")
}
if y is not none {
    print("got something")
}
match y {
    Some(v) -> print_int(v)
    none -> print("nothing")
}

is not Pat reads as one operator — is negated by the trailing not — and works anywhere is Pat does (expression context and the if … is … form). It's the predicate spelling of "does this not match"; for the if form, the body runs when the pattern does not match.

is and is not bind like comparisons, tighter than and and or, so if ready and x is none reads as ready and (x is none). A pattern that binds a name, like Some(v), only works when the is is the whole if condition: if a and x is Some(v) is an error, since v would be unset when a is false. Some(_) or Some(_v) binds nothing and works anywhere.

Or peel off the Some with let .Some(v) = y else { ... }:

let .Some(v) = y else { return -1 }
// v is in scope and has type int64

An optional of an optional is that optional, since T? is T | none and a union is a set: with type MaybeInt = int64?, MaybeInt? is int64?, and so is T? in a generic function where T is int64?. So none means one thing. A Map[str, int64?]'s get returns none both for a missing key and for a stored none; contains tells them apart. Where the difference matters, an enum that names both cases says it better.

items.title: Postfix ?
items.text:
expr? on a T? value evaluates to T. Without a trailing clause it panics on none; with or default it substitutes the default instead:

let n: int64? = find("hello", 'l')
let idx: int64       = n?           // panics if none
let idx2: int64      = n? or -1     // -1 if none

The default is evaluated lazily (only when the value is none), and its type must match the unwrapped T, unless it's a call that never returns, such as panic(...) or a helper that ends in one (see Return values). It's built as a T: with T an interface, a struct default becomes an interface value, and with T an enum, .Up names T's variant. x? on a value that isn't optional is an error. A following or outside the unwrap stays a boolean operator: x? or 1 substitutes 1 for none, but (x?) or some_bool is a boolean-or on the unwrapped value (and a type error unless T is bool).

Operators don't look inside an optional. With n: int64?, n == 3, n < 4 and n + 1 are errors, and so is comparing a bool? such as m.get(key) with true; unwrap first, as in n? == 3 or (n? or 0) + 1. Only == none and != none compare the optional itself.

items.title: Optional chaining
items.text: On a struct T?, x?.field and x?.method(...) evaluate to an optional of the field or return type, and to none without touching the field when x is none. x?.method(...) works on any T? whose T has methods: n?.to_str() on an int64?, s?.find("l") on a str?, or a method of an interface value. A field or return type that is already optional stays one level deep, so chains read through: with a: A? whose b: B? has n: int64?, a?.b?.n is an int64?. x?.method(...) takes arguments like an ordinary method call: arguments it leaves out take the method's defaults, and none of them is evaluated when x is none. A T? doesn't stand in for a T: returning t?.name from a function declared -> str or -> str or Error is an error, so unwrap it first with t?.name? or t?.name? or "", or declare the function -> str?. t?.name = v isn't an assignment; unwrap first, as in if t is Some(u) { u.name = v }.

items.title: Arrays
items.text:
[T] is a resizable array of element type T:

let nums: [int64] = [1, 2, 3]
let names: [str] = ["alice", "bob"]

See Arrays for indexing, slicing, and concatenation.

items.title: Structs
items.text:
Named product types:

type Point = struct {
    x: int64
    y: int64
}

See Structs.

items.title: Enums
items.text:
Tagged unions:

type Shape = enum {
    Circle(radius: int64)
    Rect(w: int64, h: int64)
}

See Enums.

items.title: Generics
items.text:
Type-parametric structs are monomorphised at compile time:

type Pair[A, B] = struct {
    first: A
    second: B
}

let p: Pair[str, int64] = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42)

The type arguments of a constructor call pick the instantiation, so let p = Pair[str, int64](first: "hello", second: 42) needs no annotation. A generic struct always needs them: a bare Pair(first: "hello", second: 42) is an error that says to write Pair[A, B](...). A generic struct's method signatures are always checked, but a method body is compiled only for each instantiation, so the body of a struct that nothing instantiates isn't checked. An error in a body is reported once, for the first instantiation that hits it, and names that instantiation, like Pair[str, int64]. A type argument is a name (str, ast.Expr), an array ([str]), an optional of either (int64?, [str]?) or another instantiation (Map[str, Pair[int64, str]]()). Function types (func(int64) -> str) and optional instantiations (Pair[str, int64]?) aren't accepted. Passing the wrong number of type arguments, or type arguments to a struct that isn't generic, is an error, and so is a Type[A, B] that isn't followed by (. The same goes for a generic written as a type: let m: Map = ... is an error that says to write Map[K, V], and Map[str] is one for the missing type argument.

Map[K, V] (in builtins) is the canonical example.

Functions can be generic too, with their type arguments usually inferred from the call: see Generic functions.

items.title: Interfaces
items.text:
Method-based contracts that types can opt into by declaring the right methods. Primitives implement them implicitly via boxing.

interface Printable {
    func to_str(self) -> str
}

func show(anon x: Printable) -> none {
    print(x.to_str())
}

show(42)        // works — int64 implements Printable via primitives/int64.kod
show(true)      // same for bool

A call on an interface value must name one of the interface's methods, with arguments that match its signature; an unknown method is an error. A trailing argument the call leaves out takes the default the interface declares for it (func greet(self, times: int64 = 2) -> str), so give each implementation the same default.

A struct, an enum, int64, str or bool becomes an interface value wherever one is expected (a bytes value or a union can't be one): an annotated let, an argument, a field, an array element, a value stored with m[k] = v, and a return value, including the value of a -> Shape? or -> Shape or Error function.

The type must declare every method of the interface, with the same parameter and return types (labels and defaults may differ). Otherwise using it as the interface is an error at that spot, such as struct `P` doesn't implement interface `Shape`: missing method `area` (enum `E` ... for an enum) or method `area` is `func(int64) -> int64`, not `func() -> int64`. throw counts too, since it makes its value an Error.

An interface value converts to another interface that declares only methods the first one has, with the same parameter and return types, in any order. It goes wherever a struct would (an argument, an annotated let, a field, a return value), and a downcast still works on the result:

interface Reader {
    func read(self) -> int64
}
interface ReadCloser {
    func close(self) -> none
    func read(self) -> int64
}

func drain(anon r: Reader) -> int64 {
    return r.read()
}

let rc: ReadCloser = File(n: 7)
drain(rc)                      // 7
let r: Reader = rc
if r is File(f) {              // still the File
    print_int(f.n)
}

Converting builds the new interface's method table when it runs, so it costs a small allocation. Arrays and optionals of interface values don't convert element by element: a [ReadCloser] is not a [Reader].

items.title: Union types
items.text:
A | B holds a value of any one of its member types. A match or is says which one it holds:

type Id = int64 | str

func show(anon id: Id) -> str {
    match id {
        int64(n) -> return f"#{n}"
        str(s) -> return s
    }
}

let id: Id = 42
if id is str(s) {
    print(s)
}

A member can be any type: a primitive, a struct, an enum, an interface, an array, a generic instance or a function type. See Pattern matching for the patterns.

A union is a set, so order, repeats and nesting don't matter. int64 | str and str | int64 are one type, in every module, and with type Id = int64 | str, Id | bool is int64 | str | bool. A union with only one member left is that member.

none in a union makes it optional: T | none is exactly T?, and A | B | none is the optional of A | B, which can also be written (A | B)?. An optional member counts the same way, so A? | B is that type too. Its arms sit side by side, with no Some: A(a), B(b) and none.

In a type, | binds tighter than or, so int64 | str or Error is a fallible int64 | str. A function type's return type takes every member after the ->, so func() -> int64 | str returns a union. To put such a function in a union, put it in parentheses: (func() -> int64) | str. Parentheses group any type this way, and a ? after them makes the group optional.

A value goes into a union by being written where the union is declared, as a T goes into a T?. It goes to the member of its own type. Without one, a struct, enum or primitive goes to an interface member it implements, and implementing two of them is an error, since it could be either. An enum's .Variant goes to the one enum member that declares that variant, and [] to the one array member. A value with no member reports the mismatch (expected `int64 | str`, got `bool`).

A union goes where a union with all of its members is declared: an A | B is accepted as an A | B | C, and holds the same member there. Only the value itself widens. An [A | B] isn't an [A | B | C], as an [Sq] isn't a [Shape], and an (A | B)? isn't an (A | B | C)?; match those and put each member in instead. Nor is a union accepted where one of its members is declared.

A union prints as the member it holds, with print(x), f"{x}" or str(x), when every member can be printed. == and != compare two unions, or a union and a value that goes into it (x == 3, x == "a", x == .Red): they're equal when they hold the same member and those members are ==. Every member needs a == of its own, so a union with a struct member that doesn't declare op_eq, or an array member, can't be compared. A union widens for == as it does elsewhere, so an A | B compares with an A | B | C. A union whose members can all be hashed (int64, str, bytes, bool, enums without payloads) can be hashed and be a Map key: Map[int64 | str, V] (see hash). Otherwise a union has no fields, methods or operators of its own.

A union can mention a type parameter, in a generic function, struct or enum:

func label[T](anon x: T | str) -> str {
    match x {
        str(s) -> return f"text {s}"
        T(t) -> return f"other {t}"
    }
}

print(label(3))                  // other 3
print(label[int64]("a"))         // text a

Each instance is the union of what the parameters stand for, as a set. With T = int64 the parameter above is an int64 | str; with T = str it is just str, so label[str]("a") takes the first arm that matches, text a; and with T = int64 | bool it is bool | int64 | str, where T(t) matches an int64 or a bool and binds it as an int64 | bool (see type patterns). A call infers T from an argument for such a parameter: T is the argument's members that the parameter doesn't list, so label(3) is label[int64], and an argument of type int64 | str makes it int64 too. When that leaves nothing, as in label("a"), the type arguments have to be written.

A union alias can't refer to itself, so a recursive type such as a JSON value is still an enum.

items.title: Type aliases
items.text:
type Name = T gives an existing type a second name. An alias is transparent: a value of the alias type is a value of T, with all of its methods, fields and operators. The target can be any type, including one declared further down the module or one from the module's own imports (type Num2 = dep.Num, usable as mid.Num2 from a module that imports only mid, or type Num = dep.Num to pass the name on as mid.Num). Each module's aliases are its own: two modules may declare aliases of one name whether or not they stand for the same type, and a module's alias may take the name of a struct, enum or interface another module declares (see Modules):

type Name = str
type Ids = [int64]
type MaybeNode = Node?
type Callback = func(int64) -> int64
type StrMap = Map[str, str]
type Outcome = int64 or Error
type Key = int64 | str

type Node = struct {
    label: str
}

let n: Name = "kod"
print_int(n.char_count())    // 3

An alias of T or Error works wherever T or Error does, including as the return type of a function or of main, so throw, try and must behave the same through it. That holds for an imported alias too, written dep.Outcome or listed in import "./dep" { Outcome }.

An alias whose target names an unknown type is an error, and so is one that refers back to itself through other aliases (type A = B with type B = A). So is a target that gets a generic's type arguments wrong, such as type B = Map[str], type P = Pair or type D = [Box[int64]] for a Box that isn't generic. Each of these is reported once, at the alias.

items.title: Fallible types: T or Error
items.text:
A function declared -> T or Error returns a Result cell — either an Ok(T) or an Err(Error). Use try to propagate, must to panic, or pattern-match the result directly.

try and must take a T or Error value, and try only works inside a function that returns T or Error itself; anything else is an error. Either can appear anywhere a value can, as in out += [try parse(s)] or xs[try first(xs)..]; on an Err, try returns from the function there. An explicit Result[T, E] with an E other than Error doesn't count, since its error isn't an Error to report or pass on; match it instead.

A call whose result is a T or Error can't be used as a statement on its own, because that would drop an error without a word:

file.close()               // error: the `none or Error` result of this call is dropped
try file.close()           // propagate it
must file.close()          // panic on it
let _ = file.close()       // ignore it, on purpose

let _ = expr evaluates expr, whatever its type, and keeps nothing: it binds no name, so it can be written any number of times in a block, and _ can't be read afterwards. It is for fallible calls whose failure doesn't matter, like closing a connection that already failed. Any other value can be dropped by calling it as a statement, as before.

A none or Error function that ends without a return, or with a bare return, returns Ok(none), as return none does.

A T goes where a T or Error is declared as its Ok, the way a T goes into a T?. That holds in a return, an annotated let, an assignment, an argument, a struct field, an array element, and an arm of a match whose value goes to one of them:

let r: int64 or Error = 3                // Ok(3)
let rs: [int64 or Error] = [1, read_size("a.txt")]

A value that is already a T or Error goes as it is, and a nested result wraps as often as it takes: let r: (int64 or Error) or Error = 3 is Ok(Ok(3)). Without the parentheses, int64 or Error or Error is just int64 or Error. A failure is never implicit. An Error where an int64 or Error is declared is an error that says to throw it, or to write .Err(error: e). Only when T itself takes the value, as with Error or Error, is it the Ok. .Ok(value: 3) still works, and so does .Err(error: e).

Error is the only type that can follow or: -> int64 or IoError is a parse error. Throw a struct or enum that implements Error instead, and recover it with a downcast (see below). throw takes an Error value, so throwing an array, an optional, or an enum without a to_str is an error, such as enum `Color` doesn't implement interface `Error`: missing method `to_str`.

type IoError = struct {
    message: str
    func to_str(self) -> str { return self.message }
}

func read_size(anon path: str) -> int64 or Error {
    throw IoError(message: f"file not found: {path}")
}

func main() -> int64 {
    let n: int64 = must read_size("missing.txt")  // panics on Err
    return n
}

To inspect a result instead of propagating or panicking, pattern-match it with Ok / Err (the two-armed analog of Some / none). Ok's binding has the result's value type; Err's is the Error interface (on an explicit Result[T, E], it's an E):

match read_size("missing.txt") {
    Ok(n)  -> print_int(n)
    Err(e) -> print(e.to_str())
}

A type pattern on a result tests what it holds when it succeeded, so a result matches like the value it carries. Error(e) is another way to write Err(e):

match parse(s) {                         // -> int64 | str or Error
    int64(n) -> use(n)
    str(t) -> show(t)
    Error(e) -> print(e.to_str())
}

T(t) matches an Ok whose value matches T(t) as a pattern on the success type: a member of a union, a union or optional of several, the success type itself (any Ok), a downcast when it is an interface, and none when it is optional. A type pattern never looks inside the error, even for a type that implements Error: NotFound(nf) on an int64 or Error is an error that points at Err(NotFound(nf)), which downcasts it.

The same patterns work with if … is and the bare is operator, which is handy in tests:

let r = read_size("missing.txt")
assert r is Err(_)              // it failed
if r is Err(e) { print(e.to_str()) }

items.title: A default for a failure: ? on a result
items.text:
r? or default, r?.field and r?.method() work on a T or Error as they do on a T?. Each takes the success value, and on a failure gives up the error right there, where the code says so:

let n = read_size("a.txt")? or 0
let name = load(path)?.name? or "?"

r?.field and r?.method() give an optional, none for a failure, so a chain ends in ? or default as an optional's does. When T is itself optional, a failure and a none look the same, as for a T??. A bare r? on a result is an error: it would stop the program without saying what failed, which is what must r does with the error's message.

items.title: Recovering the concrete error type
items.text:
Err(e) binds e as the Error interface. To get back the concrete error struct, downcast with is StructType(binding) — a general interface downcast that tests the boxed type and, on a match, binds the typed value:

match read_size(path) {
    Ok(n)  -> use(n)
    Err(e) ->
        if e is NotFound(nf) {
            print(f"missing: {nf.path}")
        } else {
            print(e.to_str())
        }
}

It works in match, if … is, and the bare is operator (a match on an interface needs an else, since its set of implementors isn't enumerable). A struct that doesn't implement the interface can never be in one, so naming it is an error: `Point` doesn't implement `Shape`, so a `Shape` is never a `Point`. x is T and a T(b) pattern hold only for a value of exactly that declaration, or that generic instance, whichever module boxed it, so an error struct that an imported function throws matches its type in the caller. T may be an alias of a struct or of a generic instance (type IntBox = Box[int64]), written dep.T through another module. Naming a generic type itself (is Box) is an error: `Box` is generic; downcast to one of its instances through a type alias such as `type IntBox = Box[int64]`. The pattern names such a struct through its module (e is errs.NotFound(nf), which needs errs to declare NotFound) or, when it is imported as an item, by its own name (e is NotFound(nf)). Either way it binds one name, the struct, whose fields are read from it. A local or parameter named like the module hides it, so errs.NotFound(nf) after let errs = 3 is an error.
